INFORMA L OPENING OF GRAND LODGE
The I 45th Annual Communicat ion of the Grand Lodge of California
began with the Informal Opening of Grand Lodge on Sunday, October 9, 1994, at
2:30 p.m. in the Masonic Auditorium of the California Masonic Memorial Temple,
1111 California Street, San Francisco, California. The Grand Lodge Officers were
led in procession into Grand Lodge by Most Worshipful Warren J. Blomseth, !27th
Grand Master of Masons in California. Grand Lodge was raised for this occasion
by Edwin D. Clarke and Gaylord V. Roten, Executive Officers respectively of the
Northern California and Southern California Jurisdictions of the Order ofDeMolay.
The gavel used was a part of a matched set of burl redwood handcrafted by
Worshipful Alfred E. Price, Past Master, which had been presented to the Grand
Master at the combined I 25th Year Anniversary Celebration of Confidence Lodge
No. 203 and Salinas Lodge No. 204 on September 30, 1994.
The Grand Master wlecomed all in attendance and acknowledged with
pleasure the large attendance by the Family of Freemasonry. The Grand Master
was both pleased and delighted to have the opportunity to welcome the leadership
of Freemasonry and the general public to share in Freemasonry's vision and to
officially and formally acknowledge the 75th Anniversary of the International
Order of DeMolay.
The Grand Chaplain gave the invocation, after which the Grand Marshal
presented the Flag of the United States of America, followed by the pledge of
allegiance.
Visiting Grand Masters from other Grand Jurisdictions were then
presented, together )Vith the representatives of Grand Masters who were in
attendance. Together with the Prestonian Lecturer and the Past Grand Chaplain of
the United Grand Lodge of England. They were individually introduced by the
Grand Marshal, and then welcomed by the Grand Master.
The Grand Marshal then conducted the leaders of the concordant and
appendant bodies into Grand Lodge, and introduced each one individually. The
Grand Master extended his greetings to each one, and welcomed each one to the
session. Those leaders in attendance were as follows:

v ESPER SERVICE
The Vesper Service began at 4:45 p.m. in the cathedral, with a procession
ofGra~d Lodge Officer~, led by DeMolays from State Center Chapter, including

Each was greeted by the Grand Master, and then escorted to seats in the East. Each
then brought remarks from his or her respective organization to Grand Lodge.
The Grand Master then presented a check for $4,000 to each of the four
youth leaders for leadership training and related activities. The funds came from
the California Masonic Foundation, and from the Grand Lodge Committee on
Youth Orders.
Bro. Jim McDonald, Chairman of the Youth Orders Committee was then
introduced, and he, in turn, introduced Brothers C. Eugene McMahon, Charles G.
Abbott, and Paul Van den Brink, who had been selected to receive the Grand
Master's Youth Achievement A ward. These awards were then presented by the
Grand Master, assisted by the Deputy Grand Master, followed by the Grand Honors
of Masonry by Three Times Three.
Two DeMolays then gave a musical presentation by singing a solo each.
The first was Raymond J. Martinez Ill, and the second was Donnell Dowell, Jr.
Their presentation was greeted enthusiastically by the assembled guests. The
Grand Master noted that their musical program was a perfect way in wh ich to
celebrate DeMolay's Diamond Anniversary Year.
The Grand Marshal was then instructed to escort the Deputy Grand Master
of the Most Worshipful Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Inc., to the East.
Bro. Joseph V . Nicholas as asked to bring greetings from his Grand Lodge, and
also to introduce his officers present, which he did. His remarks were greeted with
a strong round of applause by the assembled guests. Grand Master Blomseth in his
response stated, "Our common love of Freemasonry draws us together" and
extended best wishes for the continued health and prosperity of the Prince Hall
Grand Lodge, its officers and members. The Grand Master then presented Brother
Edwin Clarke and Gaylord Roten with special presentation awards in honor of their
service to DeMolay and in recognition ofDeMolay's 75th Anniversary Year.
The Informal Opening of Grand Lodge was then concluded, and the
assembled guests invited to join the Grand Master and Grand Lodge Officers across
the street at Grace Cathedral for the Annual Vesper Service.

a bagpiper. The processional was "Amazing Grace." The Invocation was offered
by the Grand Chaplain, followed by a musical selection by Bro. Mark Harris,
Master of Oriental Lodge No. 144. A reading from Scripture followed by the
Grand Orator, Bro. J. Lloyd Clayton, followed by another musical selection by
Heather R. Cooper, wife of the Grand Secretary.
After another Scripture reading by the Grand Secretary, and a hymn of
special importance to the Grand Master and Mrs. Blomseth ("Great Is Thy
Faithfulness"), the message was brought by Dr. Michael Morgan, Past Grand
Chaplain of the United Grand Lodge of England. Another musical selection a
duet, concluded the service, and after the benediction by the Grand Chaplain, th~se
in attendance followed the Grand Master back to the Memorial Temple where
everyone enjoyed an Old Fashioned Ice Cream Social in the Exhibit Hall.
Of special importance on this occasion was the music, including the
recessional hymn, which was by Bro. Jean Sibelius, and which had been originally
written by him to celebrate the bringing of Freemasonry to Finland in the period
after World War I, and which music had been given to the Grand Lodge of New
York in appreciation for the role that Grand Lodge had played in Finnish Masonic
history.

The 145th Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of California was
opened at 9:00 a.m. in the Masonic Auditorium of the California Masonic
Memoria l Temple in San Francisco by Most Worshipful Warren J. Blomseth,
Grand Master of Masons in California. At the appointed hour the Grand Lodge
Officers marched in procession into the auditoriu m, after Grand Lodge was raised
by Wor. Bro. Larry C. Richardson, Master of Tri Square Lodge No. 551 in
Hayward (the Grand Master's Lodge), using an African padauk wood gavel and
sounding block which had been handcrafted by Bro. Malcolm R. Savage, a member
of Tri Square Lodge No. 551 , and presented at the "Grand Master's Day" on
October 30, 1993, at Hayward .
Before the Opening of Grand Lodge, the Grand Master asked the Grand
Secretary to call the roll of Grand Lodge Officers, Past Grand Masters, and Past
Grand Officers, as well as to announce the report of the Credentials Committe e on
the number of registered delegates in attendance. The following answered the call
of the roll:

GRAND CHAPLAIN'S MESSAGE
The Grand Master then called on the Grand Chaplain to deliver a message
to Grand Lodge. Worshipful Emile R. Laversin then delivered an inspirational
address.

Grand Chaplain
Most Worshipful Grand Master, My Fellow Grand Lodge Officers,
Dist inguished Past Grand Masters and my Bre thren all.
YOU - yes my brother - YOU, I am speaking singularly to each and every
one of you, and of course I must include myse lf - we can make a difference - yes
ONE man alone can make a difference.
My brethren you have heard our Grand Master speak of the Challenge of
Change and the Rewards o f Renewal. As your Grand Chaplain thi s year, I wo uld
like to touch upon the personal and moral ethics of our Grand Master ' s theme.
As Masons, we go among o ur peers, with many of them aware that we are
members of the Masonic Fraternity, and we should at a ll times be consc ious, that
by our own actions we can bring great credit or disgrace to our Fraternity - that, my
brothers, is a tremendous responsibility we all have. It surely is not what we think
or say about ourselves, but how others perceive us. It is not a ride on a ··merry-goround" , trying to get the gold ring, but rather it is choosin g a pathway lined with
Jove and truth.
I would like to re late to you the personal experience that brought me to
Masonry. In the wan ing years of my father's life, on the occasion of a visit with

Dad, you' re not a Mason are you?" "No," he replied. Then, I asked. ''Why is it
you suggest I look into joining the Masons?"
" Well," he answered, - and herein my brethren lies the essence of my
message - when he said quite simply, "in my years as a consulting engineer l came
across many different men, and the few that I admired most because of their
integrity and honesty came to be known to me as Masons, and I liked the ir answers
to my questions." He then named several men, whose nam es I've since forgotten,
but remembered that he had spoken of th em with admiration . My fa ther's
convincing sincerity led me within three months to seek adm iss ion. whi ch fo r the
last 48 years has sustained me we ll.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

LEO E. ANDERSON
Eulogy
by Myron E. Smith, PGM

As we embark upon this moment of tribute to the memory of our departed
Brother, Most Worshipful Leo E. Anderson, Past Grand Master of Masons in
California, for a text, two passages of scripture ftom the rule and guide of our faith
seem particularly appropriate:
"And you, like the lamp, must shed light among your fellows, so that,
when they see the good you do, they may give praise to your Father in
heaven."
- Matthew 5:16
"I have fought the good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the
faith; henceforth there is laid up for me a crown ofrighteousness, which
the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day ... "
- Timothy 4:7,8
The memorial impulse is one of the great forces for good in life; it is the
impelling desire to remember and to be remembered. Leo was well aware of the
significance of the memorial impulse. Often, he stood at this podium to eulogize
Brethren of other years who had joined the Great Grand Lodge on High and now,
in tum, we remember him and honor his memory.
This is a heartwarming experience. There are so many things to remember
about Leo. Friendship for more than half a century brings countless memories to
mind. There are five points of remembrance which are especially meaningful:
Leo's unwavering Faith in God.
His stalwart Advocacy. ·
His Enthusiasm.
His Humor.
His Leadership.
LEO E. ANDERSON
Past Grand Master
February 20, 1902 - October 20, 1993

Gettysburg, South Dakota is the place where Leo was born, on February
20, 1902. When he was three, his parents moved with him to California.

14

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

In 1919, he was valedictorian of his graduating class at Huntington Park
High School.

. Leo was initiated , passed and raised in Hollywood Lodge No. 155,
becommg a Master Mason on January 29, 1931. He was elected Master of his
Lodge in 1938.

In 1924, he graduated from the College of Commerce at the University of
Southern California.
In 1927, he graduated from the School of Law at U.S.C. and was admitted
to the Bar. He began practice with Meserve, Mumper and Hughes, becoming a
member of the fmn in 1938 and soon it's managing partner. He practiced law until
1989 when he retired after 62 years.
In 1933 he married the beautiful Hollis "Holly" Norris. They became the
parents of a daughter, Denise, and a son, David. They were saddened by the
demise of their daughter in her youth. Their son, like Leo, became an attorney,
now practicing in Santa Barbara.
Not many years after their daughter's death, Leo's wife Holly passed
away. Following long sorrow, Leo married again - a lovely woman named Polly,
but, sadly, she also preceded Leo in death and he was destined to live his sunset
years alone.
Leo's business interests were many:
President -

Midler Avenue Realty and Building Corporation in
Syracuse, New York.

Vice President - Lennox Industries, Inc., Marshaltown , Iowa.

15

Leo served the Grand Lodge in many capacities on many committees. He
rendered distinguished service as our Grand Orator in 1940, as Inspector for seven
years, and as Grand Master from September 27, 1957 to October 3, J958.
As Grand Master, Leo dedicated this beautiful new California Masonic
Memorial Temple, erected in memory of our Brethren who lost their lives in the
cause of freedom . For many years, he was appointed Chainnan of the Committee
on Jurisprudence, where he was instrumental in clarifying the California Masonic
Code.
Leo was a member of the York Rite, the Scottish Rite and Al Malaikah
Shrine Temple. The Supreme Council coroneted him with the Honorary 33 ° and
in 1968 he was Potentate of Al Malaikah Shrine Temple. He was a member of the
Order of Constantine.
Leo passed away on October 20, 1993. Memorial services were
conducted in the Wee Kirk O' the Heather, Glendale, California. Dr. J. Whitcomb
Brougher, who had been his Grand Chaplain, officiated. Brother Ralph H. Head,
who had been a co-trustee with Leo on the Trust that contributes to Masonic
Service Bureaus, assisted Dr. Brougher, telling about Leo's Masonic activities.
All of these events and activities put into force our five special points of
remembrance of Leo:

Secretary
Treasurer -

Saybroon Corporation, Los Angeles, California.

l.

Leo's humanitarian activities included:
Trustee -

The Los Angeles Philanthropic Foundation

President -

Board of Directors of Forest Lawn Memorial Park
Association

Chairman -

Board of Directors of Shriners' Hospital

Trustee -

Masonic Homes of California

Trustee -

Trust benefiting the Masonic Service Bureaus

Added to all of these activities, Leo was for 53 years the consul for the
Republic of Latvia in Los Angeles.

2.

3.

Leo's faith in God . When the believer shines to th.e praise of
God, he sends a communication out into the world by his words,
deeds and spirit. So it was with Leo. He had a presence that
reminded you that each of us is a child of God and you felt
inspired and strengthened to be with him and to work with him .
Leo's stalwart advocacy. There was a symbolism in Leo's birth
in a town named Gettysburg. Leo was a great intellectual
warrior. He planned well; he did his homework. In the
courtroom, he was a powerful adversary. Likewise, around the
conference table and here in this Grand Lodge you soon learned
to be certain whereof you spoke before you took issue with Leo.
He commanded your respect with his native ability to make clear
and understandable complex and complicated subjects and
problems.
Leo's enthusiasm. The philosopher and theologian, Ralph
Waldo Emerson, said nothing great or important is ever achieved

5.

without enthusias m . The word comes from the Greek that
means "The Divine in Us." Leo kept this special light glowing
and invariably instilled new enthusias m in all around him and
near him.
Leo's humor. Like Mark Twain, Leo used human interest
anecdotes to lift the spirits of his Brethren. It was good to see
the sparkle in his eyes when he related a humorous story to
illustrate a serious point of view.
Leo ' s leadership . Leo truly was a great leader. In his
professio n, he was known and respected across the country in
many corporate settings for his professional expertise; in
business life his acumen was phenomenal ; and in Masonry he
was loved and respected for his geniality, his friendship and his
constant willingness to serve his Brethren and the Grand Lodge.

To visualize fully the scope of these points of remembrance of Leo, we
to look to the closing paragraph and prayer in his Grand Master's
only
need
as
Message Grand Master in October, 1958, in which he said:
'The English language is entirely inadequate to express to you, my
brethren, the pleasure and the pure happiness I have experienced this past
year. Only the privilege of meeting and working with the members of this
great fraternity can bring these great rewards of friendship with fraternal
love and affection to others. Wonderful and lasting memories of
kindness, hospitality and good fellowship come flooding over me as I
close this report of my year as your Grand Master. I wish I could find the
words to express to you my gratitude for the privilege and honor you have
given to me. I can only hope that you can read between the lines and see
into my heart, for there you will find indelible pictures of all of you.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

27

FIRST BUSINESS SESSION
The first item of business brought before Grand Lodge by the Grand
Master was a consideration of Grand Master's Recommendation No. I and Grand
Masters's Recommendation No. 2 as emergent legislation. Recommendation No.
J changed the order of business for the Installation of Officers from the last item
of business at the end of the session to the last day of the session, regardless of
when the business was concluded. Recommendation No. 2 adopted Rules of Order
for the conduct of this and all future Annual Communicat ions.
The Deputy Grand Master was asked to take the Grand Master's Station
for the following motions, which were made by the Grand Master:
It was moved, seconded and unanimously carried to permit the
introduction of these two Recommendations as emergent legislation. It was moved,
seconded and carried to adopt Recommendation No. 1, and then again moved,
seconded and carried to adopt Recommendation No. 2. The Deputy Grand Master
declared the two Recommenda tions adopted, and in consequence thereof that the
Installation of Officers would take place on Wednesday, October 12, and that the
Rules of Order just adopted as Recommendation No. 2 would govern the
proceedings of the 145th Annual Communicat ion and all future Annual
Communications.

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
The Grand Master then relinquished his station again to the Deputy Grand
Master for the purpose of delivering his Grand Master's Message. The message
was divided into two parts, the first being a summary of all his official acts for the
year and a report on the general condition of Masonry within the jurisdiction, and
the second being his official Recommendations which were taken up separately
later in the session. A copy of the complete Grand Master's Message is found in
Appendix "A" (except for the Recommendations, which are found in Appendix
"H").

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

"The Challenge ofChange - The Rewards ofRenewal"
As I now stand before you I would thank God for providing me
throughout my life with an abundance of great teachers and magnificent mentors.
And I would thank God for His gracious guidance and His strong hand of strength
which has enabled me to accomplish the tasks set before me.
umnony Prevails

APPENDIX A

By way of a general observation I would confinn once again that hannony
prevails among the craft and throughout the Family of Freemasonry. No
contention exists except for that natural and healthy rivalry which motivates us all
in the perfonnance of our duty and our responsibility. Each and every member of
the family ofFreemasonry strive to be ever faithful to the sublime principles and
tenants of Freemasonry. Your Grand Master could not be more pleased.
As but one example: This year for the first time in the 69 year history of
the East-West Shrine Football Classic - your Grand Lodge Officers together with
the Masters of our Lodges were invited and marched in the Pre-game Parade. What
a wonderful example of fraternal goodwill, mutual support, and regard. The vision
of harmony prevails.
Wbat to Expect
Bro. Sir Wa1ter Scott who became a Freemason in 1801 (193 years ago)
stated in one of his letters :
"There is a Freemasonry among kindred spirits that always leads them to
understand one another at little express of words."
This my Grand Master's message will likewise endeavor to lead this Grand
Lodge to a better understanding of the Craft" ... at little express of words."
In preparing this message like all of my messages I gave considerable care
to the choice of words. This was done in an effort to communicate in the clearest

and most concise manner possible. The exact word is important if one's true
meaning is to be conveyed and readily understood.
My very favorite story in this regard is no doubt a favorite of everyone
·
who has heard it Noah Webster's wife came suddenly into the pantry and caught Noah
embracing the chamber maid -

42

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

"Mr. Webster," she exclaimed, "I am surprised,"
The great compiler of our most famous dictionary gave his wife a look of
reproof "No, my pet," he replied "you are amazed. It is we who are surprised."
I trust that before I complete this, my Grand Master's message, that you
may be properly amazed but not surprised.
A Matter of Principle
It is most o ften just as well to deal with the negative or with
disappointments at the off-set and without delay.
In keeping with the concept of Brotherly Love and of Relief to those in
need I issued two calls for our lodges and members to come to the relief of our
brethren who suffered great losses as a result of the substantial damage from the
Northridge Earthquake of January 17th 1994. The response from other Grand
Lodges, Lodges and Organizations outside of California was truly exemplary. Our
own California Scottish Rite responded most generously. However less th an 25%
of o ur Lodges responded. Those who did, did so in substantial amounts which
averaged $400 per lodge. The remaining 75% of our lodges have yet to respond.
Where is the vision?
A Matter of Concern
Due to a combination of fortuitous circumstances as the result of:
excellent asset management; consolidations; or through bequests, wills, estates and
trusts; many of our lodges have sizeable assets generally held in investment
portfolios. Regardless of the total sum (whether it be under $50,000 or over
$500,000) the importance to the lodge and its members cannot be over stated.
The duty and responsibility of the Master, Secretary and Trustees to
ensure asset preservation, a fair return and reasonable growth is an absolute
requirement.
Quite recently one of our lodges suffered a major loss of assets due to :
lax auditin g and financial control procedures;
dishonesty leading to embezzlement;
forgery; and fabrication of financial statements.
Although the loss had already been sustained a newly elected Master

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

43

exercised his duty and responsibility with great skill by instituting required controls
takin g legal action and mitigating some of the loss through recovery from
insurance. He has my personal commendation and appreciation.
There are several others of our Lodges which have or are experiencing
similar financial troubles although not now as extensive. However, my brethren,
the potential is present in many of our lodges. Clearly lodge asset management,
regardless of the asset value, requires application of the "prudent man rule"
together with appropriate procedures, lodge over-sight and comprehensive checks
and balances.
Your Grand Lodge Insurance Committee under the direction of Bro. Dave
E. Tavemetti, Chairman, will be immediately providing every lodge with written
material and somewhat later a comprehensive checklist applicable to both our
lodges and our temple or hall associations.
This written material will identify duties and responsibilities for lodge
leadership and lodge trustee as well as hall or temple directors. And explain the
various actions each need to take. Additionally there will be guidance with regard
to insurance coverages which should be considered. The checklists will assist in
evaluating exposure and confirm that appropriate actions have and are being taken.
These checklists will also be used as a reference by our Inspectors as they perform
the annual lodge audit. But more importantly they need to be utilized by every
lodge to ensure that all necessary and required steps are taken to safeguard lodge
and temple or hall association assets and to further ensure the proper exercise of
fiduciary responsibilities on behalf of the lodge.
Should you have any immediate concerns in this regard contact your
Inspector or Worshipful Bro. Tavernetti or our Grand Secretary. Every vision
·
requires a sound financial foundation.
Appropriate Dues Structure
There is a related issue which, I believe, also warrants thoughtful
consideration.
A number of our financially secure lodges, again, most often the
benefactors of bequests or consolidations, or both, have chosen to lower or sustain
very low dues rather than utilize their precious investment income to build the
Lodge and the Craft through charitable and community involvement programs.
One example: $20 dues with a budget equal to over $100 per member - and no repeat no - charitable or community involvement programs. Where is the vision?
What role do our principles play when we use income derived from the labor of
yesterday's Masons to pay today's operating expense and in that process cheapen
our fraternity and cheat today's members of their rightful role to carry their fair

44

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

share of today's cost and to support today's programs and activities which affirm
who and what we are!
Again, the challenge is yours as is the decision to act or !121 to act. To
grow our fraternity or n..Q1 to grow it. My Brethren we were not founded to shirk
either our Masonic duty or Masonic responsibility. Where is our vision?
Grand Master's Decisions
Before this Communication is over you will have noted that there are no
Grand Master's decisions.
Grand Master's decisions are as you know,
interpretations of our current law which address a specific issue during a Grand
Master's year and serve as a guide to future Grand Masters. But such decisions are
not binding upon future Grand Masters. They may accept or reject such
interpretations as they may choose, and rightly so, for conditions change.
I am of the personal opinion that we presently have a sufficient body of
law which over time ought to be reduced not expanded. That we should endeavor
to conduct and handle the majority of our business administratively based upon
well defined and carefully crafted policy statements and clear, concise procedures.
Accordingly, I issued no new decisions. I conducted the work and
business of the office of the Grand Master utilizing existing CMC law. In most
instances, conflicts or concerns were assigned to the Grand Master's Personal
Representative, the Inspector, working with and through the Assistant Grand
Lecturer. In other words, the purpose and the goal was to solve the problem at the
lowest possible level where the maximum knowledge exists and where proper and
early resolution has the highest priority. The Grand Master's role is to ensure
justice and fairness within the confines of our law.
The four Assistant Grand Lecturers and the one hundred and twelve
District Inspectors are to be commended for and supported in their ever expanding
administrative role.
Does ever more law contribute to the vision and mission of this our
beloved fraternity? I for one, think not!
Resolutions
On Tuesday we will take up a fairly large body of resolutions for
consideration and legislative action. Since your legislative packets were mailed a
few resolutions have been formally withdrawn (for which I thank the proposers).
One I asked the proponents to withdraw. They chose not to do so. And one I ruled
out-of-order prior to the preparation of the packet mailed to the lodges.
That resolution would have asked the delegates to consider and approve

G RAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

45

the relocation of your Grand Lodge.
That resolution would have posed the wrong question and would, if
passed, have had a negative impact upon this Grand Lodge that would be
impossible to measure.
If this Grand Lodge in its infinite wisdom desires to seriously consider
relocation it must do so by creating a blue ribbon study committee and provide that
committee with initial funding of at least $100,000 to cover special study costs,
such as survey, cost analysis and funding reports by property specialist, engineers,
architects, facility managers and like professionals.
Further, as Grand Master I view such resolutions as unworthy of a
fraternity whose founders had a vision and to which many, many generations of
Masons contributed. They built this structure as a memorial which we now hold
in trust. We must keep the faith and fulfill the promise. This building is a symbol.
And in and of itself is yesterday's, today's and tomorrow's vision of what and who
we are!

Mason of the Year.

On the evening of September 29th we celebrated the fifth of our members
to attain the rank and status of Mason of the Year in our Grand Lodge's 145-year
history.
Most Worshipful Donald B. McCaw's extensive biographic and Masonic
history fully qualifies our worthy brother for the honor of Mason ofthe Year.
Brother Don's past service to the Grand Lodge, to the Masonic Homes, to
Jurisprudence, to this Memorial Temple, and to the California Masonic Foundation
would be sufficient to qualify him for this award.
But quite honestly, the cap stone of Don's service has been and is his role
in the formation of and initial several year's operation of Nob Hill Masonic
Management Inc. (Known affectionately as "Nob Hill").
Simply stated, Nob Hill was conceived, formed, chartered and now
functions as a for-profit corporation in the operation and management of the
Masonic Auditorium, Exhibit Hall, Parking Garage and Pine Street Properties.
Don is serving as its first President and guiding spirit.
That is a rather simple statement. But that simple statement can be readily
translated into several thousand hours of dedicated and devoted labor - all freely
given. Labor to be defined in this instance as highly professional talent - that of a
very competent lawyer and manager.
No one of us could possible calculate the value of Don's donated time to
our beloved fraternity. It has truly been a labor of love and such a labor deserves
to be richly rewarded although rarely is it properly acknowledged let alone given

The title and award of Mason ofthe Year is but a small token of our love,

J l.

Feeding 01;iportunities.
Here's an observation:

One of the deadly sins identified for business by Peter F . Drucker is also
a deadly sin for our personal lives, for our fraternity and its lodges and for our
Grand Lodge. That deadly sin is - " ... feeding problems and starving
opportunities."
There is a tendency for leaders within any organization to put their time
and talent and, yes, energy into problem solving which, in turn, starves the
ooportunities.
"Problem-solving" is really and truly just damage -containment. Only
opportunities produce real change and real growth.
It sounds simple and it really is simple. But it will make all the difference
in the world to your future and the future of your Lodge and this Grand Lodge.
I try really hard to identify and act upon at least one opportun ity each
week. Incidentally leadars know that with opportunity development you most often
find yourself facing considerable risk. Exploiting opportunities usually involves
risk and a fair share of failure. Most ofus, if not all of us, find risk uncomfortable
and failure an embarrassment. We are not alone - the greatest success stories in the
history of mankind confirm that risk taking and significant failures are the
foundation for most, if not every success story.
Be not afraid of failure - do not avoid risk seeking or risk taking. Rather
set out to nourish every opportunity for you and for your lodge in its development
and growth . Always putting quality and excellence first - as primary
considerations. Build quality and excellence into ritual and into every program and
every event. Let your vision be one of feeding opportunities.

In the five year period from 1989 to 1994 our membership declined by
37, 138 members for an average decline of 4.66% per year. Unless we make some
major changes and significant choices during the next four years (from 1995 to
2000) our membership could and no doubt will decline by an estimated 30,000
members for an average decline of 4.9% per year. This latter estimate is based on
well established historic membership patterns measured against Hewitt Associates
suggested actuary tables.
I doubt if you anymore than I, want to project those figures out twenty
years from today at 5% plus membership loss per year. That's just not acceptable.
Your leadership has another vision - a vision based upon renewal. And
that renewal process has already begun.
One September 9th and I 0th at three locations throughout California 722
Masters, Wardens, active members, committeemen and Grand Lodge Officers
attended one of three two hour-long Masonic Renewal conferences. It was an
historic event.
Those who attended and participated were challenged. They were taken
over a rough and rugged road and made to face our fraternity's future - squarely
and unflinchingly. And they were given the first glimpse of a new vision for their
lodge and this Grand Lodge for the year 2000 and beyond.

and I also shared two thoughts concerning renewal - Renewal being the keystone

73

REMARKS CONCERNING
THE 1995 GRAND LODGE BUDGET
William F. Stovall, Deputy Grand Master
Much has been said about the financial health of our Grand Lodge, but it
can all be summed up in the following: For years, expenses exceeded income. To
meet this annual shortfall, reserves were expended each year until ALL of our
reserves were depleted. The Grand Lodge began borrowing funds each year just
to meet current expenses, and that borrowing occurred earlier in each succeeding
year.
This condition could not be permitted to continue. To correct this
practice, major changes needed to be made in our financial structure, financ ial
reporting, financial planning and financial accountability, as well as in our
organizational structure and long term goals.

APPENDIX B

I am pleased to report to you that changes in those areas have come a long
way. In 199 1 we began developing, and now have in place, a six-year financial
plan for our Grand Lodge, a plan which ensures financial responsibility and allows
the flexibility for a managed reduction in operations without a major disruption in
the services of our constituent lodges. This plan now represents a long-term
solution rather than a quick-fix to the constraints imposed upon each succeeding
Grand Master by a decline of 6,000 members each year in the face of ever
increasing unit costs of business.
On August 29, 1994, after a review and approval by the Finance and
Executive Committees·of the Grand Lodge, every California Lodge was mailed a
copy of my proposed budget for the Grand Lodge year c.ommencing November l ,
1994. And for the fourth consecutive communication, the proposed net budget
continues to decrease while it stays carefully within the revenues collected.
In addition to providing for the operational and ceremonial expenses of
our Grand Lodge, this budget proposes to accomplish four major goals for next
year:
I.

It completes the pay-back of the $700,000 which was required to run our
Grand Lodge business between July 1992 and November 1992. This cost
was incurred when the fiscal year was changed and no revenues had been
collected to adjust for this expense.

2.

It establishes important reserves for certain cyclical expenses such as
depreciation/replacement for our large capital items.

3.

It initiates and capitalizes a Grand Lodge Endowment Fund which will

74

PROCEEDINGS OF THE ·

generate additional revenues over the years to help offset the increased
costs of operations.
4.

And it incorporates a conservative estimated dividend from our Nob Hill
Masonic Management Corporation, which was fonned as a for-profit
corporation to market our properties on Nob Hill and, from its business,
to provide operating revenues in the fonn of dividends to our Grand
Lodge.

Yes, there have been major changes in the structure and operations of our
Grand Lodge, but there is yet much work to be done.
Since 1991, your Grand Masters and elected officers have made you a
commitment each year to control the Grand Lodge operations and bring to it a
responsible fmancial management. We have kept the faith. We have a plan. The
plan is good. The plan is working to restore our financial stability. And, the plan
should be continued as we restructure our Fraternity to meet the challenges of the
future.
I am grateful for your past support, and I now ask you for your continued
support by your approval of the proposed 1995 Grand Lodge Budget, which the
Finance Committee will now present to you for your action.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

REMARKS AFTER INSTALLATION
Grab the Gold Ring
by William F. Stovall, Grand Master
Have you ever said to yourself, "Gee, what a great opportunity that was,
I'm really sorry I missed it?" Most opportunities are not missed because we don't
know about them. It is more likely that we just weren't sure, we didn't have enough
information, we are afraid of the uncertainties and hesitated to grab them while
they were in front of us, or we thought they would take too much work. Thomas
Edison said, "Opportunity is missed by most people because it is dressed in overalls
and looks like work." There is much truth in that statement.
When I was a child my parents would occasionally take me down to the
old Pike Amusement Zone on the beach at Long Beach. I really looked forward to
riding the merry-go-round and one of the best things about the merry-go-round was
the opportunity to grab the gold ring that could be exchanged for a prize.
Not every ring was gold. In fact, most of them were some kind of silvercolored metal, but we all knew that we had the opportunity to grab a gold one. I
remember that I had to lean way out while the carousel was picking up speed and
my horse was going up and down in order to reach the rings. The kids who played
it cautiously and only leaned out when they were certain they were grabbing for the
gold ring usually missed it as it passed by.
But the kids who leaned out and tried to grab a ring on every trip around
usually ended up with the most gold, and usually had the most fun. These kids
learned a valuable lesson in life: they had learned to make the most of their time
by taking advantage of every opportunity presented to reach their goals.
Freemasonry in California stands today on the threshold of great
opportunities, the opportunity to demonstrate to our communities that strengths and
good works of our Fraternity, or the opportunity to wring our hands about our
declining, disinterested membership, to grumble, complain and fmd fault. The
choice between the opportunity to become involved or the opportunity to sit back
and wait for someone else to solve our problems, which is just not going to happen.
It is time to be brave, to start grabbing the rings, to grab every opportunity
that we can, to be seen, to be heard and to make a difference in our country. We
need to shake loose from our old constraints and become a relevant force in our
communities once again. Why do I say "once again?"

Sometimes I get the feeling that many of our lodges are in some kind of
semi-conscious state with regards to the things that are happening around them.
Either that, or they just don't care.

APPENDIX C

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

REPORT OF THE SENIOR GRAND

81

wARDEN

Per Capita Recommen dations for 1995-96
Brethren of the Grand Lodge:

APPENDIX C

Legislation adopted at our 1993 Annual Communic ation charges the
Deputy Grand Master with the preparation of a budget covering his anticipated year
as Grand Master. Of necessity, this preparation must begin during his year as
Senior Grand Warden, as the per capita which you act upon at this Annual
Communication will be for our 1995-96 Grand Lodge year. Preliminary work on
the 1995-96 budget was begun several months ago.
As you know from the communication sent to your Lodges by our Deputy
Grand Master on August 29 of this year, we are again supporting a 4% increase in
the per capita for the 1995-96, with a portion of that increase to be allocated to our
publication , The California Freemason. Rising costs, particularly the virtually
certain increase in postal rates, makes it impossible to avoid increasing the
allocation to that publication .
As was also stated in our Deputy Grand Master's communica tion to you,
th is will leave our Grand Lodge with a smaller operating revenue than for the
previous year. Your Executive Committee pledges itself to continuing the concept
of shared sacrifice. Therefore, although the per capita increases, it will be
matched, as it has been for the past several years, by reductions in the operating
costs of your Grand Lodge equal to the revenue lost by declining membershi p.
This will continue to be accomplish ed by careful oversight and tight control of all
Grand Lodge expenditur es.
After consultation with representation of the Grand Lodge Finance
Committee , who will present this to you for adoption in their report, we ask for a
total per capita for the 1995-96 Grand Lodge year of $15 .49, of which $1 . 16 will
be allocated to the California Freemason.
I might add that the increase for the California Freemason is not likely to
cover the anticipated increased costs, but the California Freemason will probably
have to be subsidized by allocation from operating revenue. This has already been
considered in the preliminary budget planning.

APPENDIX D

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

85

REPORT OF THE GRAND T REASURER

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The Grand Treasurer is charged with the responsibility of reporting to the
members of this Grand Lodge on the financial condition of Grand Lodge and its
entities, which include the Masonic Homes of California, the California Masonic
Memorial Temple, the California Masonic Foundation, and the Nob Hill Masonic
Management, Inc. (please refer to the opinion letters attached hereto by your
auditors).

APPENDIX D

The reports and comments of the Grand Treasurer are based on the official
examinations and statements of our Certified Public Accountants whose reports are
an integral part of the Grand Treasurer's Report. Their audits cover the years most
recently ended and contain a complete record of income and expenses for the
period.
The delegates to the Annual Communication are, in effect, the
stockholders of the entities of Grand Lodge and you are encouraged, and it is
recommended, that you read and review this report. Your observations are
appreciated.
Both the Grand Lodge and each of its related entities are in sound
financial condition. The extent and size of our charitable activities were financially
possible inlarge measure due to the generosity of prior generations. To assure the
future of these fine programs we must continue our Masonic tradition of financial
support.
Respectfully submitted,
Henry H.P. Wilkins, Grand Treasurer

APPENDIX E

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFOR NIA

175

REPOR T OF THE GRAND SECRET ARY

Dear Brethren:

APPENDIX E

Once more I must report to you that the Grand Lodge of California has
fewer Lodges and fewer members than the year before. We now have 461 regular
Lodges, plus four research Lodges. We now have 125,160 members , and 122,2 59
assessible members, the number on which the budget is based . The loss of
members is somewha t related to the loss of Lodges, but not exclusively. The
changing nature of our populatio n, is in part responsible, because a number of
Lodges that were formerly located in the downtown areas of the major metropolitan
areas have difficulty sustaining themselves as their members move away from the
area. However , an even more important reason is the difficulty that Lodges have
in obtaining qualified officers each year. This is not a problem that the Grand
Lodge Office can address, but it is being addressed elsewhere, especially through
the Masonic Renewal Program and o ur Wardens' Retreats.
During the period ending June 30, 1994, we initiated 1,489 Entered
Apprentices, passed to the Degree of Fellow Craft 1,117, and Raised to the Sublime
Degree of Master Mason l, 175. But our net loss due to deaths and resignations
since my previous report a year ago, and which were not made up by new Master
Masons, is 4,075. It is this figure that we use to estimate our losses from one year
to the next. It should be noted that if we had more Entered Apprentices and Fellow
Crafts advancin g, we would have more Master Masons automatically.
The Grand Lodge Office continues with its stafT reduction plan and with
the upgrading of services provided. The "800" number has grown in popularity,
and the use of this "toll-free" number has quadrupled. While this is an additional
cost to be absorbed in the Grand Lodge Office, I believe that this is a benefit to our
Lodges and to our Secretaries. We a lso worked with the Homes Board and with
the Memorial Temple Board to refurbish the rest of the Grand Lodge Office,
something not done since 1976. The result is a much better working environment,
and full complian ce with current laws on employee working environment.
The Board of Trustees of the Homes added a Director of Human
Resource s to their stafT this year, and she is located at the San Francisco Office.
This reflects an additional effort to serve the Masonic Homes of California, which
is a substantial part of the responsibility of the Grand Secretary's Office.

My thanks go to all those who helped make this year a successful one for
the Grand Lodge Office.

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
The duties of the Grand Lecturer are prescribed in our Masonic Code.
Accordingly, this report will recount the activities of the committee
throughout the year.
The usual Spring Conferences were held in all four divisions, and the
work performed reflected the effort directed toward uniformity and confonnity to
our established ritual. Also during the year the Assistant Grand Lecturers and the
Inspectors conducted schools in their divisions and districts respectively.

APPENDIX F

Many years ago our beloved Past Grand Master Alfred F. Breslauer wrote
in "The Master's Handbook", quote "We should never lose sight of one important
fact. There is nothing in Masonry more important than the ritual when a degree is
being conferred. In other words too much time can never be spent in making
officers competent to confer a degree in an impressive and intelligent manner". In
this context our Inspectors throughout the year gave unstintedly of their time and
talents to bring the proficiency of the officers under their charge up to that degree
of perfection. Yet there are conditions in a number of our lodges which are not
considered health y. In most instances the Inspectors by counseling with the
officers and brechren have been instrumental in taking positive steps to alleviate the
existing conditions.
Fifteen Seminars were held throughout the jurisdiction during this Grand
Lodge year. I am most pleased to report that the interest along with the good and
sometimes great attendance has proven the effectiveness of this program.
On September 28th I had occasion to visit Maya Lodge No. 793. The 2°
was being conferred for the first time in Spanish . The euphony of the language
coupled with the accuracy of the floor work was most impressive. Congratulations
to the translators, to the Officers, to Worshipful James Paden, the Inspector for that
Lodge for all his efforts. To Worshipful Arthur Hernandez, Inspector, who assisted
in the translation. To all the Brethren of Maya Lodge whose efforts have brought
their dream into fruition. Congratulations - gracias MIS Herxanos.
In closing, my personal thanks to our Grand Master and his wife Dee, for
all the courtesies extended to me throughout the year along with the warmth of
their friendship . To the rest of the "team" who have acquitted themselves so ably
in our ceremonies. and for their everlasting friendship, my thank you.
To our candidates and offic.ers coaches, your efforts are deeply
appreciated.

21 6

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

To our Inspectors, and to those who have served in that capacity who are
laving or have left us during the year, no expression of gratitude can be adequate.
To my colleagues on the committee, your efforts have not gone unnoticed.
My sincerest and profoundest thank you - to Richard Andrews of Division
II, who leaves the committee at the conclusion of this session. We wish you God
speed, and we thank you, for all your efforts under must difficult geographical
conditions.
To the Grand Secretary and his entire staff for their continued and
valuable assistance, my sincere thank you.
And finally, to you my brethren, for allowing me the privilege to serve our
fraternity, my humblest thank you.
Respectfully submitted,
Ulysses G. Patropulos, Grand Lecturer

GRAND ORATION
J. Lloyd Clayton, Grand Orator
Most Worsh ipful Grand Master, Past Grand Masters, Distinguished
Masonic Visitors, Fellow Grand Lodge Officers, Brethren All.
It has been a most edifying experience to be a Grand Lodge Officer, and
at the same time, a most rewarding and exciting time in my Masonic career. I wish
to thank our Grand Master, Most Worshipful Warren Blomseth, for the opportunity
to serve this Grand Lodge as Grand Orator. My thanks also, to my fellow Grand
Lodge Officers who rallied behind me at every event, always with words of
encouragement and support.

APPENDIX G

I would be remiss if I did not express my appreciation for the aid and
assistance given me by the Assistant Grand Lecturers, the Inspectors and Lodge
Officers in the many districts where the Grand Lodge was called upon to perform
the various ceremonies. Without the local history and background supplied by
those dedicated Masons, the task of preparing addresses for the functions would
have been much more difficu lt.
The last two years have been a most trying time for the Masonic Family
as once again we have been under attack by anti-Masonic factions, who seem to be
dedicated to the eradication of our great fraternity. Although we appeared to have
gained a victory, I am afraid that we have not dissuaded them , we have only
temporarily averted their attack. Let us review some of the anti-Masonic history
of our order.
Our late Bmther John J. Robinson, was a writer with a special interest in
the history of Medieval Britain and the Crusades. In his research into the history
of Medieval England, he was surprised by the constant trails that the early
Freemasons left in the sands of time. His main interest was, of course, the England
of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. With his curiosity peeked by the thread of
Masonry woven through the history, he began concentrating his study on th e
activities of the Knights Templar.
The Knights Templar was fonned in the days of the crusades, when
pilgrims, on their way to the Holy Land were set upon by bandits and highwaymen.
The Knights Templar provided safe passage to these travellers, and as a
consequence, became wealthy and powerful people.
John Robinson determined that there was no doubt in his mind that the
secret society which came to be known as Freemasonry, had been born out of the
society of mutual protection formed by the Knights Templar and their associates
in Britain.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

As history has shown, conflicts have grown between powerful groups
throughout the ages. ln early Europe, the religious groups were in the position of
great power, and the kings and rulers of the European countries were under the
control of various religious factions. The power accumulating to the Knights
Templar became a threat to some of these religious groups, and the result was an
attempt to destroy the Knights Templar.
The public became aware of Freemasonry when four Masonic Lodges in
London formed the Grand Lodge of England on June 24, 1717. It did not take too
many years to pass before, in 1738, Pope Clement XII issued the first of many
bulls, or orders, from the Catholic Church denouncing Freemasonry as an
adversary or threat to the church authority, and forbidding membership in
Freemasonry by any member of the Catholic Church. The succession of bulls
continued as Pope Benedict XIV renewed and continued Clement's Constitution.
Pope Pius VII followed them both. Pope Leo XII, by his Apostolic Constitution quo graviora - recapitulating the acts and decrees of the previous Pontiffs about the
matter, validated and confirmed them forever. Jn the same way, Popes Pius VIII,
Gregory XVI, and very often Pius IX continued in the same vein.
The Masonic Order moved to the new world with the first immigrants to
this country. Those members were very much in evidence as the struggle for
independence progressed, and the United States was formed. Freemasonry, it soon
became evident, had not left the antagonists and reactionaries behind.
There were certain anti-Masonic sentiments apparent in the first years of
our country. Such groups as the Quakers, the Mennonites, Moravians and
Lutherans opposed membership in any so-called "secret society."
In 1826, the episode of the William Morgan Affair unfolded. Although
no record can be found to confinn that William Morgan ever took the three degrees
of Masonry, the records of the Western Star Chapter No. 35 in LeRoy, New York
reveals that Morgan petitioned for the degrees of Royal Arch Masonry and was
exalted to the Royal Arch in May 1825. He was involved in the forming of a new
Royal Arch Chapter in Batavia, New York, but for unknown reasons his name was
stricken from the roll.
Whether this prompted him to develop anti-Masonic sentiments, or for
some other reason, no one will ever know, but within one year he authored an
expose of the secret rituals of Freemasonry entitled "lllustrations of Freemasonry."
Several attempts were made to stop the publication of the book, but apparently he
had entered into partnership with others, and he no longer was in control of the
book he had authored.
It is reported that a mysterious fire consumed the print shop where the
book was being published. Morgan claimed that the Masons were responsible for
the fire in order to stop the bool<'s printing. Then out of the blue, Morgan was

arrested on charges of theft. There are no documents detailing exactly what
occ~ed aft~r.the arrest, but Morgan was released from jail on September 12, 1826.
Outside ~e Jail'. Morgan entered a carriage. It is questionable whether he entered
volunt~nly or 1~voluntarily, but his whereabouts can be traced to Fort Niagara.
~here is .no reliable account as to his presence after September 19, 1826. He
simply disappeared.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Traditionally, it has been the practice of the Masonic Fraternity, to refrain
from engaging in any public debates on the merits of our order. This silence has
been misinterpreted by some to reason that Freemasonry has something to hide, or
that .its principles are flawed. Nothing could be further from the truth. This
Masonic practice of turning the other cheek has only encouraged more criticism.
I think a precedence was set last year when such a strong stand was taken against
our detractors. In the words of Illustrious C. Fred Kleinknecht, 33°, Sovereign
Grand Commande r of the Southern Jurisdiction of the Scottish Rite, "Masonry
provides a philosophy and a fraternity where good men can 'meet on the level and
part on the square.' It binds all en in a mystic tie of sincere brotherhood and mutual
love. Faith and work, soul and body, heart and hand are united as Masons
everywhere labor through Freemasonry in peace and hannony to honor the Creator
and serve mankind. Such are the objectives of Freemasonry."
My Brothers, it becomes incumbent upon all of us to increase our
knowledge of Freemason ry. There is ample printed material available on the
teachings and history of the Masonic Order from this Grand Lodge, from the
Scottish Rite, from the York Rite, and from numerous Research Lodges in this and
other jurisdiction s. Many of our Lodges and concordant bodies maintain
outstanding libraries where thousands of books on Freemasonry are available to us.
We must continue our education of Freemasonry, that we may become better
informed, and thus more capable of responding to the misinformation which is
shouted against us.
Not everyone has the ability to write lengthy articles, compositions or
our Fraternity, but I was particularly pleased to read those articles in the
on
essays
Scottish Rite Journal by such celebrated Masons as Dr. Norman Vincent Peale;
Abner V. McCall, President Emeritus of Baylor University; John Edwin Johns,
President of Furman University; Past Grand Master R. Stephen Doan; Bishop Carl
Sanders; and Rabbi Sidney S. Guthman. Our own Grand Master, Most Worshipful
Warren 1. Blomseth, along with most of our Past Grand Masters of California have
contributed inspiring and informative articles to this and other publications on the
subject of Freemasonry. It is through essays and papers such as those presented by
such prominent and influential Masons who have the power of persuasion to be
able to set the record straight, that Masonry can hope to defuse any potentially
explosive situations before they become menacing. While it is incumbent on such
influential Masons to continue to defend Masonry, it is also incumbent on each and
every one of us to increase our knowledge of the Order.
I therefore challenge everyone present today to improve your personal
library, to seek out the many good books and publications dealing with
Freemasonry, to read and study them that you might become more informed about
our Fraternity, and, in turn, to share the knowledge you have acquired with your

225

fellow Lodge Brothers. To the Masters and Wardens, I challenge you to organize
a short educational program to be presented at your Stated Meetings which would
help educate all your members about the history and character of Freemasonry.
You may find that such a program might not only improve the members knowledge
of the Craft, but might also help to improve the attendance and participation at your
meetings.
Starting today then, my Brothers, let us rededicate ourselves to the
advancement of our education and enlightenment of the Fraternity, so we can stand,
unflinching , in the face of any assault by our adversaries.

During the past few years, Grand Lodge Week has decreased from an
original five days to two days of business, plus a third day for the Installation of
Officers. The present Code section governing the installation of Officers requires
the installation to be the last item of business on the last day of the session. But the
past two years, Grand Lodge has voted unanimously to suspend this rule so that
business can be concluded the day before the Installation of Officers. The current
law is archaic, and needs to be changed pennanently without having to ask Grand
Lodge to suspend the rules each year to temporarily change it. It is therefore my
recommendation that the law be changed to pennit the Installation of Officers to
take place at a time and place as detennined by the newly-elected Grand Master
If you adopt this recommendation, the sixth paragraph of Section 510 of
the California Masonic Code will be amended to read as follows:
The Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Grand Wardens,

elected by wrinen ballot .!ls. 6ft the final ~item of business
before the installation of said officers at each Annual
Communica!ion. A majority of the votes cast shall be necessary
for an election. Grand Lodge may, by unanimous consent,
permit any designated officer to cast the ballot for Grand Lodge.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Section 510 of the California Masonic Code governing the installation of
Officers requires the election to be held on the final day of each Annual
Communication. For the past two years, the Grand Lodge has unanimously
approved to suspend this rule, so business could be concluded the day before the
final day of the Comm unication.

emergent resolution by amending Section SI 0 of the CMC to permit the Installation
to take place as determined by the Grand Master-elect.

change is consistent with the present Grand Lodge policy.

Recommendation No. 2
Adopts Permanent Rules of Procedure
For Annual and Special Communications
The Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of California is the single
most important event in the Grand Lodge Year. At the Annual Communication
the delegates to Grand Lodge exercise their powers as the deliberative and
legislative body of this organization. As such it is important that the Rules of
Procedure be understood by all voting delegates, and that these procedures be
consistent, clear, as well as fair to all concerned .
The 1993 Annual Communication the Grand Lodge of California operated
under Rules of Procedure drafted by then Grand Master R. Stephen Doan and the
Committee on Jurisprudence. These procedures provided for an orderly
environment in which to deliberate on all legislative matters before us. It is
therefore my recommendation as Grand Master that these rules of procedure be
adopted by the Grand Lodge so that we have systematic guidelines to govern us at
all future Annual Communications.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following new Part V will be added
to the Ordinances of the Grand Lodge as contained in the California Masonic Code:
PARTY
RULES OF PROCEDURE FOR ANNUAL
AND SPECIAL COMMUNICATION S
The following Rules of Procedure shall govern the deliberations at each
Annual and Special Communication of the Grand Lodge.
All committee reports must be in the hands of the Grand Secretary by the
close of business on the first day of the Communication. Legislation shall be heard
at the sessions on the second and subsequent days of the Communication. Each
chairman of a committee to which legislation has been referred should be present
at all times during the sessions at which legislation will be considered until all
reports from his committee have been given. Ifa committeeman is not present and
prepared to report when called for, the Grand Secretary shall read the committee's

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

231

report. If the Grand Secretary does not then have a copy of the report to read, the
vote will be taken without that report.
The Jurisprudence Committee shall report only once, unless there is a
special matter before the Grand Lodge which the committee and presiding officer
believe warrant individual attention. The presiding officer shall announce the vote
required for passage of each item before discussion begins.
Any legislation to be considered which has not been mailed to the Lodges
shall be printed in advance and distributed at or before the session at which the
matter shall be considered. No legislation may be modified at any time without the
consent of the proponent or his authorized representative written on the face of the
modified proposal. If any proposal is modified after it has been made available to
the delegates, any changes must be clearly brought to the attention of the delegates
at the Grand Lodge session by the presiding officer. If not so presented by the
presiding officer, the proposed modification shall ~be a part of the adopted
legislation.
The Grand Secretary shall not read the minutes of any session during the
Communication. The minutes will be printed instead in the proceedings of the
Annual Communication.
When discussion of each resolution or other item of business is called for
by the presiding officer, the proponent, or his authorized representative, shall have
the option of speaking first or last. The proponent shall be allotted five minutes.
All other speakers from the floor shall be allotted three minutes each.
If the proponent speaks first, a speaker opposed to the matter shall speak
next, and the pro ll!ld con speakers shall alternate thereafter. If the proponent
chooses to speak last, a speaker in opposition shall begin the discussion, and the
speakers shall alternate thereafter. Only three speakers on each side of an issue,
including the proponent, shall be pennitted on each item under discussion.
Speakers in favor shall speak from the microphone on the Grand Master's left.
Speakers opposed shall speak from the microphone on the Grand Master's right.
There shall be no lights on the floor nor shall any speaker's microphone
be cut off. There shall be signal lights at the Grand Master's station. The presiding
officer shall advise the speaker when his time has expired and request that he
immediately conclude his remarks.
If circumstances or the issue under discussion warrant, the presiding
officer, in his sole discretion, may waive any of the guidelines set forth above. For
example, the presiding officer at his discretion may grant speakers additional time
or may give more than six speakers pennission to present their views. It is
contemplated that the waiver of these rules would only occur on issues of great
importance to the Craft.

Recommendation No. 3
Clarifies Language Relating to Masonic
Communication with Non-Recognized Masonic
Freemasonry in this country has been moving steadily toward a better
understanding of the issues of "recognition" and of "exclusive territorial
jurisdiction" for Grand Lodges. California has been a participant in this movement,
and the Grand Lodge has approved the recommendations of two Grand Masters in
the past five years to reflect this new understanding. The language we use reflects
our ability to reach out to and understand others. Old terms such as "clandestine,"
with their negative connotations, have become obsolete. It is much more accurate
to describe other Masonic organizations with which we are not at the present in
fraternal communication as being "non-recognized." It is therefore my
recommendation that the California Masonic Code be amended to delete this
obsolete language, and replace it with language that reflects our current
understanding of the status of other Grand Lodges which share our Masonic name
and heritage.

Recommendation No. 7
Provides ror Disposition or Pre-Paid Dues
Upon a Lodge Consolidation
The present Masonic law in California is not clear as to the obligation to
refund dues that may have been overpaid when two or more Lodges consolidate.
If one Lodge had higher dues than the newly consolidated Lodge, the Brethren in
the new Lodge are treated unequally if money is owing to some, but not to all.
This can be easily changed by revising the California Masonic Code to require a
refund where a refund is due to a Brother. It is therefore my recommendation that
this new language be adopted.

Masonic Code will be amended to read as follows:

debts of each Lodge. The oro rata portion of the dues
paid in excess of the dues established by the
consolidated Lodge shall be either refunded to the
member or. at bis discretion. credited as dues paid in
advance. The Past Masters and life members of each
Lodge become such of the new Lodge.

of a visitor, authorized by the Master'', introduces an ambiguity which, we believe,

Recommendation No. 9
Revises Terminology on "Burden of Proor• at Masonic Trials
Masonic trials are not criminal trials. They are more nearly like civil trials
in that the results of conviction can be exclusion from the Fraternity, either
temporarily or permanently. In a criminal trial, the "burden of proof' is
considerably more difficult than in a civil trial. lt is my belief that our current
language should be revised to conform to the meaning of "burden of proof' in a
civil trial, which is the "preponderance of evidence" rule, rather than "proof beyond
all reasonable doubt" rule. This definition is simpler to use in Masonic trials and
more nearly approximates how our Masonic law works .
If you adopt this recommendation, the following paragraph will be added
to the end of Section 32320 of the California Masonic Code:
The accuser has the burden oforovjng by a preponderance of the
evidence all of the facts necessary to establish the existence of
ynmasonic conduct on the oart of the accused. "Preponderance
of the evidence" means evidence that has more convincing force
than that opposed to it. If the evidence is so evenly balanced that
one is unable to say that the evidence on an issye preponderates.
the burden has not been met.
Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master has recommended that in Masonic trials the evidence
necessary to convict a Mason of a Masonic offense be reduced to "preponderance
of evidence" from "beyond a reasonable doubt."
Such evidentiary proof is simpler and Jess convincing than in a criminal
trial. It is the opinion of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes that this
change in the burden of proof in Masonic trials is well founded and proper.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

239

Report of the Committee on Trial Review:

Grand Master's Recommendation No. 94-09 which has been referred to
your Trial Review Committee, compares the burden of proof in criminal cases to
the burden of proof in civil cases in our courts, and concludes that since Masonic
trials are more like civil trials than criminal trials, the burden of proof in Masonic
trials should be by, "preponderance of the evidence" as in civil cases rather than,
"beyond a reasonable doubt" as in criminal cases.
This would be the first time a definitive standard of proof has been spelled
out in our California Masonic Code. It appears from previous trials that sometimes
one standard has been used and at other times the other.
Since this addition to our Code substantially clarifies the standard of proof
required in our Masonic trials, your Trial Review Committee recommends a "Yes"
vote.
Recommendation CARRIED-OVER.
Recommendation No. 10
Changes Requirements for Ritual Changes
The California Masonic Code presently contains an archaic and inaccurate
statement about our Ritual. It states that the Ritual can be changed, but can only
be changed to "restore" it to the Ritual that has existed from time immemorial. But
no one can clearly demonstrate today what that Ritual is. Masonic Ritual has been
in a constant state o( evolution for as Jong as we have any evidence for it. The
Code Revision Committee has therefore recommended to me that I propose a
change in the law to reflect historical accuracy. This section would require that our
Ritual be changed the same way that other laws are changed, which is in fact what
we have always done. The proposed revision would clear up an inaccuracy in our
written law, and clarify what is now an ambiguity.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 263 10 of the California
Masonic Code will be amended to read as follows:

§26310. CHANGE OF RITUAL.

amendment to these Ordinances.

Report ofthe Com mi/lee on Policy and General Purposes:
There is a restriction in our law (CMC 26310) that the Ritual may be
changed only in order for the purpose of having it remain as it has been handed
down from time immemorial. This recommendation proposes to remove that
restriction.
Before taking such an action we should ask ourselves why the restriction
has been a part of our law for so many decades.
Ritual is the great constant in Freemasonry. It is the very framework, even
the foundation of the Fraternity. The Great Architect of the Universe gave man
certain immutable laws of nature. His laws give us the reliability of the Seasons,
the tides, the course of the stars in the universe -- all without change. This
reliability has given man the ability to develop his reasoning and his responsibility
to himself and to others.
Our Grand Lodge has enjoyed many decades of men responsible for the
Ritual and its teaching to others. These men have preached that the Ritual not only
should be uniform in our jurisdiction, but should be constant. Every effort has
been made through the years to keep the Ritual in its original adopted form, and
though there is no physical proof that it is, in fact, entirely unchanged this alone is
insufficient reason to subject the Ritual to constant change. Change of the Ritual
could subject it to eventual corruption. At each Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge there could be several proposed changes in Ritual. In a relatively
short time, the Ritual adopted by our founding fathers would not be in its original
perfect and unperverted form. It would not be long before no one would know
what is the current Ritual of the Grand Lodge. Also changes to the Ritual would
result in costly changes to the adopted Cipher code, which, if not reprinted with
each change or group of changes, would not reflect the £Ymn1 Ritual.
This proposal is not in accord with the Policy and General Purposes of the

L~~e. Although the former is not a paid position, and the latter will not be a paid

position after October, 1994, there are still costs associated with those appointive
offic~rs_ that could be eliminated. It is my recommendation that these two positions
be ehmrnated at the close of the 1995 Annual Communication. The 1994/95 Grand
Lodge Year would be the last year in which these two appointive officers would
be a part of the Grand Lodge Appointive Line.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to
the California Masonic Code effective as of the close of the 1995 Annual

Recommendation No. 12
Permits Any Master Mason Who Has Sat in Lodge
With an Entered Apprentice or Pellow Craft
To Accompany Him to Another Lodge

At the present time, an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft who wishes to
visit another Lodge, can be vouched for only by a Master Mason who witnessed his
initiation or advancement. This Recommendation will allow a Master Mason who
has sat in Lodge with an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft to vouch for them.
The policy of Grand Lodge has not been to discourage visitations to
another Lodge by Entered Apprentices or Fellow Crafts, but to exercise reasonable
caution in permitting such visitations.

244

Current Masonic law in California only pennits an Entered Apprentice or
Fellow Craft to visit another Lodge when accompanied by a Master Mason who
was present when he received his degree. This proposal would pennit any Master
Mason who can vouch for an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft to accompany
him to another Lodge. A Master Mason may presently vouch for another Master
Mason ifhe has sat in Lodge with him. This would pennit a Master Mason who has
sat in Lodge with an Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft to vouch for him in the
same manner.

This Recommendation will ease the limitations on visitations without
interfering with the need for prudence.
This Recommendation is consistent with current Grand Lodge policy.
Recommendation ADOPTED.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Recommendation seeks to ease the restrictions on visitations to
another Lodge by Entered Apprentices or Fellow Crafts.

Section 16050 of the California Masonic Code requires a Lodge to hold
its Stated Meeting in a location as fixed in its Charter. Section 161 l 0 provides that
a Lodge may change this meeting place temporarily, or permanently, by following
certain procedures. However, there appears to be no provision for a Lodge to
regularly hold its Stated Meeting at more than one location. If a Lodge were
permitted to do so , it wou ld have what is commonly termed a roving charter,
although it more accurately might be described as a charter with more than one
location.
In the past, Lodges in some jurisdictions have held such charters,
particularly military Lodges. However, California has apparently never had this
practice. Some Masonic Organizations permit roving charters. For example, the
Grand Council of Cryptic Masons in California specifically permits such charters.
There are Lodges in California that would like to meet regularly in more
than one location. Sometimes this is the result of a consolidation of two Lodges
who wish to maintain the Masonic identity in two communities. Sometimes this
is the result of the desire to preserve a historic meeting place.
It is therefore my recommendation that our law be amended to permit a
Lodge to hold its Stated Meetings in more than one location, if due notice is given
to the members in writing of the location of each Stated Meeting through the usual
means of communication, such as the Lodge trestleboard.
If you adopt this recommendation, a new Section 16 I 15 will be added to
the California Masonic Code to read as follows:

such acceptable locale is "another lodge room," a generic tenn that describes a

Historically , Lodges in other jurisdiction s have had the capability to
maintain multiple meeting places concurrently. This was a particular necessity for
Lodges composed primarily of military personnel. There are also Lodges in
California which, for reasons of availability , regularly hold their Stated Meeting at
one location and Special Meeting(s) at another.
With some consolidations, the subsequently fonned Lodge has found itself
possessing more than one building, even buildings in different communities. For
historical or sentimental purposes, or simply to maintain a presence in separate
communities, some Lodges in California have expressed to the Grand Master the
desire to obtain roving charters. Certainly as consolidations become more
commonplace, such problems will arise more often. It would help to simplify the
innate complexiti es of future mergers if a capability for flexibility in the site for
Stated Meetings was available during the negotiation process.
Concern might be raised that the use of multiple meeting sites would
prove to be confusing to the membership. However, given the fact that Lodges are
already successfull y meeting at different sites at different times and that written
notice must be provided when another site is used, this is unlikely to become a
problem . Concern might also be raised that a Lodge could submit a very lengthy
list of sites in order to avoid ever having to go back to Grand Lodge for occasional
dispensations. This fear should also prove to be groundless, as the Grand Master
must approve the original submitted list.
Since individual Lodges can meet at other locations for non-Stated
Meetings, it is a logical extension to allow the same practice to apply to Stated
Meetings, ifthe members of a particular Lodge so choose. The Recommendation
is consistent with Grand Lodge Policy.

Recommendation No. 14
Permits Stated Meetings in the First Degree
As an historic perspective, it is duly acknowledged that, throughout the
formative years of Freemasonry, Entered Apprentices made up the bulk of the
membership in our Fraternity. Fellow Crafts and Master Masons were rare. In the
I 840's many Grand Lodges in the United States revised their rules to require
Lodges to bold Stated Meetings only in Lodges of Master Masons. Originally done
to encourage all Masons to become Master Masons, it eventually resulted in the
exclusion of Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts from the core life of their
Lodges. Contemporary Masonic experience teaches us the importance of including
Entered Apprentices and Fellow Crafts whenever possible in the life and activities
of the Lodge.
Jt is my finn belief that most Stated Meetings should be open to Entered
Apprentices and Fellow Crafts, with only balloting for candidates and election of
officers being reserved for Master Masons.
