Recommendation No. 15
Expands List of Those for Whom a Masonic
Funeral May Be Conducted

The attendance of an Entered Apprentice at a Stated Meeting may have
two adverse effects. First, Master Mason members may feel restricted in discussing
issues of a confidential nature in the presence of an Entered Apprentice. Would
you be required to excuse Entered Apprentices with other visitors, if confidential
matters are to be discussed among members only? Secondly, while most Stated
Meetings do not involve confidential matters or matters unfit or improper for the
ears or eyes of an Entered Apprentice, one might ask whether an Entered
Apprentice might be dissuaded from further advancement after he has witnessed
a few Stated Meetings.
You need to be convinced that both the Lodge and the Entered Apprentice
can benefit from this proposed change in a long-established practice. It is not
something that should be tried as an experiment.
The Grand Master's
Recommendation provides that the Lodge may vote to return to the practice of
holding Stated Meetings on the Master Mason degree, ifit desires. The committee
believes that this option, like many other options that are proposed at Annual
Communications, results in non-uniformity of the practice of Freemasonry in
California, and is contrary to the General Purposes of the Fraternity.
There is an element of discrimination in not allowing Entered Apprentices
to vote on candidates and election of officers but allowing them to vote on other
matters, especially matters of finance. The restrictions may embarrass the Entered
Apprentice and the permission to vote on other matters may be resented by Master
Masons.
The Committee is obligated to infonn you that the proposed change is
inconsistent with the present Policy.

Report of the Committee on Finance:
Your Committee on Finance sees no measurable financial impact on
Grand Lodge if adopted.
Recommendation CARRIED-OVER.

253

Currently an Entered Apprentice or a Fellow Craft may receive a Masonic
burial with the use of the Masonic Funeral Service, but only when authorized by
the Master of the Lodge. This was a half-way measure, adopted a number of years
ago. Before that time, only Master Masons were entitled to a Masonic burial. Now
that Entered Apprentices are considered to be members of the Fraternity, although
not yet entitled to the full privileges of a Master Mason, this section has become
obsolete. It would be rare for a Master to deny burial to an Entered Apprentice or
Fellow Craft when requested to do so.
In addition, there is archaic language referring to dueling, which should
be removed, and obsolete language requiring the Master and Wardens of a Lodge
to decide on whether or not to permit a Masonic burial for a suicide victim. In the
latter case, compassion for the brother and his family should govern, and burial
should occur no manner how the death occurred.
If you adopt this recommendation, the following changes will be made to
the California Masonic Code. Section 23090 of the California Masonic Code will
be amended as follows:

§23090. ENTERED APPRENTICES AND FELLOW

open in a degree taken by them, and the right to advancement
therein after satisfactorily passing a strict examination in open
Lodge. They may, with the consent of the Master, visit another
Lodge working in a degree taken by them, if accompanied by a
Master Mason who witnessed the initiation or advancement of
the visitor.

Recommendation No. 16
Authorizes Special Committee to Study Whether to Permit
Lodge Sponsorship of Bingo Games
The Grand Lodge of California has received increasing requests and
proposa ls for Lodges in this jurisdiction to be allowed to play bingo as a social
function in connection with meetings of the Lodge. In addition, requests have been
received to permit the renting of our Masonic centers and halls to organizations
which play bingo as a fund raising activity as allowed by local ordinance . There
is much confusion as to what the law allows, and much confusion as to how the
current California ~asonic Code should be changed, if at all, to accommodate
these requests.
Accordingly, it is my recommendation that the Grand Lodge authorize the
Grand Master to form a Special Committee to Study the Subject of Lodge
Sponsorship of Bingo Games, and to report its recommendations to him before the
1995 Annual Communication. This Study Committee could survey our Lodges to
find out the extent of interest in the playing of bingo as a purely social activity, the
extent of interest in sponsoring bingo as a fund raising activity (to the extent
permitted by law), and the interest in renting our halls and centers to outside
organizations for the same purposes. The committee could also conduct an
exhaustive investigation into what is allowed under current California law, and
recommend to the Grand Master appropriate legislation that would be in the best
interest of Freemasonry in California, and fully compliant with the laws of the
State.
There is no need to amend the California Masonic Code to implement this
proposal, and a simple majority vote is sufficient to adopt it.

This year the Grand Lodge will consider carryover legislation which
would, if passed, require our candidates to learn questions and answers. These
Historic Proficiencies are based upon the current, and much longer, proficiencies
in use today in the Grand Lodge of California. However, I believe that we would
be better served if we were to simply require our candidates to learn only the
obligations, the signs and the modes of recognition, leaving all other Masonic
teaching to Masonic Education in general, and to a series of pertinent written
questions which each candidate would be asked to answer to demonstrate his
understanding of the degree through which he has just passed .
It is my proposal, also, that this change be retroactive, so that any Entered
Apprentices or Fellow Crafts, who may not have advanced because of not having
learned the lengthy proficiencies presently required of them, may be returned to
active participation as members of our Lodges. While the numbers may vary from
Lodge to Lodge, the numbers of members that could be restored to membership
might be significantly large in the aggregate.

This proposal is contrary to the Policy and General Purposes of the Grand

In recent years, there have been several proposals to reduce or modify the
requirements of the Ritual isofar as candidates' lectures and proficiencies are
concerned. Frequently, we are told that the number of candidates who stagnate and
fail to advance is due largely to the lengthy and difficult proficiencies required of
them. If this were entirely true, it is a wonder that Masonry has existed for as long
as it has in this and other jurisdictions.

We are told that some of our sister jurisdictions do not have the stringent

requirements would produce more members, nor are we bound to follow the
policies of other jurisdictions.

Recommendation CARRIED-OVER.

We should be reminded that our great Past Grand Master Chester
MacPhee was concerned with the Masonic education of our candidates. He
frequently said that the aim was to make Masons, not merely members. Attaining
proficiency in candidates' lectures is a large step in their Masonic education, and
a step which should not be abbreviated.

In 1990 Grand Master Ronald A. Sherod appointed a committee to study
the question of recognition of the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California. That
committee has met with its counterpart appointed by their Grand Lodge since that
date, and has worked out a plan for recognition of each other's Masonic status as
a Grand Lodge, together with a proposal for visitation rights between the two
Grand Lodges. This proposal does not permit dual membership between our two
Grand Lodges, but would permit visitation of each other's Lodges and Grand
Lodges only.
A number of other American Grand Lodges, and some Canadian Grand
Lodges, have taken this important step of mutual recognition .. It preserves ~e
independence and autoaomy of each Grand Lodge, but recognizes the Masonic
status of each by permitting Masonic communication in a tiled Lodge.

If the object of California Masonry is membership, then there are other

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master recommends that we adopt a plan proposed by the
Prince Hall Recognition Committee which has been worked out with a similar
committee of the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California for visitation rights
between our two Grand Lodges. The plan does not pennit dual membership, but
permits visitation of each other's Lodges and Grand Lodges only. The proposed
change will become effective at the close of the Annual Communication following
our adoption and a similar action by the Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California.
During the 144th Annual Communication, the delegates of Grand Lodge
adopted Grand Master Doan's Recommendation No. 1 which clarified certain
ambiguities in the American Doctrine of Exclusive Territorial Jurisdiction. Grand
Master Doan's Recommendation No. I recited the American Doctrine as follows:
"There may be only one Grand Lodge in any State or Territory of the United States
unless the Grand Lodge which we recognize with exclusive jurisdiction over that
State or Territory chooses to waive its right to maintain exclusive jurisdiction and
permit concurrent jurisdiction. This interpretation is more consistent with the
theory of Grand Lodge Sovereignty: if a Grand Lodge has the right to exclude
other Masonic authorities and exercise jurisdiction over its territory, it should
likewise have sufficient sovereign power to waive that right and permit concurrent
jurisdiction." Section 220 of the California Masonic Code now reflects this
interpretation.
While this Recommendation is consistent with the policy of the Grand
Lodge with respect to territorial jurisdiction, the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes notes that there are many details regarding the visitation rights which are
not described and may result in much confusion. In the interests of clarity,
unifonnity and good Masonic relations, we feel that the proposed legislation would
be consistent with the General Purposes of the Grand Lodge if additional guidelines
are provided.

Grand Master Doan's Recommendatio n No. 5
Use of Alternate Holy Writings
What makes a man a Mason? It is his obligation. His obligation binds
him to the Fraternity. His obligation is a solemn covenant which he makes with
every man who ever has been, is now or ever will be a Mason. He promises to
support a brother in distress. He promises to aid and assist a brother's widow and
orphans. He receives the same promise in return. This covenant is so important
that our Fraternity has strict anti-solicitation rules: no man should ever have
grounds to assert that he was pressured into becoming a Mason and therefore that
his solemn covenant is somehow voidable because he was forced to become a
Mason against his will.
The importance of a Mason's obligation is evidenced by the manner in
which it is given. A man swears to God to support it and it is repeated on the Holy
Scriptures, the rule and guide of a Mason's faith . In this jurisdiction, the only Holy
Scriptures pennitted on our altar is the Christian Bible containing the Old and New
Testaments.
In Acts 4:12 of the Christian Bible, we read that no person can be saved
unless he or she believes in Jesus. Jews obviously believe otherwise. Should we
ask a Jew to make a solemn covenant on scriptures which some would interpret to
mean that a Jew cannot go to Heaven? In Luke 9:20 of the Christian Bible, we read
that Christ is the Messiah. However, Muslims believe that Christ was a prophet
only and not the Messiah. Should we ask a Muslim to make a solemn covenant on
scriptures proclaiming a Messiah in which he does not believe?
I am a committed Christian. But I am also committed to the Masonic
principle of toleration for the views of others. Just as I would want my Christian
beliefs respected, I respect the beliefs of Jews, Muslims and other non-Christians.
If given a choice, I would choose to take a solemn obligation on a Christian Bible,
and not on the Old Testament alone or on the Koran . Should not our Jewish and
Islamic friends have the option to choose their holy writings when they become
Masons? Should not every man be permitted to take his Masonic obligation on the
Volume of the Sacred Law of the faith to which he subscribes? I recommend that
you give him that right.
This proposal has been before Grand Lodge in the past. However, on each
prior occasion, various committees have recommended that you not approve it
because sufficient safeguards were not included. I believe that the following

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

263

conditions on the selection of alternate Holy Writings respond to those concerns.
I therefore recommend that every man be given the right to select alternate Holy
Writings on which he will be obligated, but only under the following
circumstances:
I.

lfa man does not wish to be obligated on the Christian Bible, he
must select alternate Holy Writings from a list promulgated from
time to time by the Grand Master of the Holy Writings of other
recognized religions. The Grand Master's list shall at all times
include the Holy Writings of those of the world's major religions
whose theology is not inconsistent with a belief in a Supreme
Being and a future existence. In selecting alternate Holy
Writings, the man must state that the book chosen is the Holy
Writings of his religious faith.

2.

The particular book selected for use on the altar during the
ceremonies of a man's degrees must be of a suitable size as
detennined by the Ritual Committee.

3.

Grand Lodge will make available all books on the list. Grand
Lodge will loan any book on the list upon request to a Lodge
which requires it for a degree.

4.

The book selected should remain on the altar throughout the
meeting during which it is used for a man's degree. However, if
a Lodge schedules more than one man to receive a degree at a
meeting and all men receiving a degree on that occasion will not
be obligated on the same book of Holy Writings, then the book
should be changed when the Lodge is at refreshment between the
degrees.

5.

When alternate Holy Writings are used during a degree, a closed
Holy Bible of any size must be on the altar.

6.

Alternate Holy Writings may be used only at a Lodge meeting
during which a man selecting the alternate Holy Writings
receives a degree and on no other occasion.

7.

Most importantly, there will be no change in the wording used
in the Ritual during the ceremonies: the words "Holy Bible" will
be used in a generic sense referring to the Holy Writings then
present on the altar.

These standards are consistent with the generally accepted ancient landmarks of
Freemasonry.

On prior occasions, it has been reported to you that several, eminent
religious scholars have studied this issue and concluded that no change was
necessary. In their view, because no right thinking person could object to the
ethical standards set forth in the Christian Bible, no man should object to its use
during his Masonic degrees.

I believe that every good Mason should respect each of the Old and New
Testaments, the Koran and all other Holy Writings. However, the issue is not
respect. The issue is the solemn covenant which each man makes on scripture.
That covenant is sacred. Because it is sacred, the candidate should swear to it on
the Holy Writings which he holds to be sacred. I ask that you give every man this
right with the safeguards set forth in this recommendation.
If you adopt this recommendation, a new Section 26295 will be added to
the California Masonic Code to read as follows:

Last year the Grand Master proposed a change in our California Masonic
Code so that a candidate could be obligated on Holy Writings other than the Holy

directed to the basics of the religious beliefs that each candidate professes and the
"holy writings" that set forth those beliefs.

recognized 1717 foundation in England under the "Christian Holy Writings. "

all masons or men are of same religious persuasions, yet they are accepted.
Therefore, to be obligated on the "holy writings" of their faith seems appropriate.

Grand Master Doan's Recommendation No. 6
Restoration of Historic Proficiencies

work, and they should from time to time recite our current candidate's lectures at
special Lodge meetings, much like they were recited in the Eighteenth Century and
before.
ln theory, a candidate should advance once he has demonstrated skill in
two areas: recognition and education . Once a candidate has learned the historic
proficiencies to which I propose that we now return, he will be equipped to
recognize and be recognized by regular Masons, whithersoever dispersed. The
portion of our current candidate's proficiencies now proposed for elimination does
not, in my opinion, give much educational value for the considerable period of time
required for its memorization. If you adopt this recommendation, a more effective
educational tool would take its place. Our candidates would be required to study
the teachings of our fraternity associated with each of the degrees and then answer
a series of written questions appertaining to the craft as the Grand Master may
promulgate from time to time.
This recommendation was developed with the assistance of the Grand
Lecturer, the Grand Secretary, the Deputy Grand Master and Grand Wardens, all
of whom join me in asking for your support of it. Should you adopt this
recommendation, we believe that you will restore the candidate's proficiencies to
their oldest form, require the candidate to memorize all that he will ever need to
pass an examination before visiting another Lodge and, most importantly, provide
a far more effective means by which our candidates may be taught what it means
to be a Mason.
If you adopt this recommendation, a candidate will be required to
memorize only those portions of the candidate's lectures as shall be exemplified
before Grand Lodg@ at this Annual Communication. ln addition, Section 26340 of
the California Masonic Code will be amended to read as follows:

Many of the projects which I have undertaken this year as Grand Master
may be summarized in three words: back to basics. We have encrusted Masonry
with much over the decades which serves no present purpose. In the process, we
have often lost sight of what we have come here to do. A case in point is our ·
California candidate's lecture in each of the three degrees.
The elaborate lectures which our candidates learn today are of relatively
recent invention in their present form. Many believe that our fraternity developed
from the medieval stonemasons guilds whose members built the great Gothic
cathedrals of Europe. These were simple men who needed a simple system by
which they could positively identify themselves to brothers and potential employers
in a foreign country . They thus developed certain signs, words and tokens which
only they themselves knew. Because many of them could not read nor write, these
modes of recognition were memorized.
When the craft began to admit men to membership who would not work
as operative Masons but who joined to study or rather speculate on the ethical
teachings associated by the stonemasons with their working tools and techniques,
ceremonies or rituals were developed. These included lectures to explain our
legends and symbolism. The lectures themselves were expanded over time. We
owe much of our present ritual to Brother William Preston whose lectures obtained
great popularity and replaced the older, simpler lectures then in use.
Men, then, as now, are reluctant to throw anything away. The old
lectures, which were given in question and answer form, were assigned to the
candidates to learn in addition to the simpler and far older proficiencies. Thus
arose the requirement that our candidates memorize not only the historic
proficiencies which we inherited from operative Masons but also the displaced
lectures given to but not theretofore memorized by the candidates. With the
passage of time, it now requires the Masonic scholar to discern the ancient from the
modern in our candidate's lectures.
I believe that it is now time to return to our historic proficiencies as they
existed during the time of George Washington and Benjamin Franklin. Our
candidates should be required to memorize only those parts of the candidate's
proficiencies which are the most ancient and which have been sufficient to prove
a man a Mason "from time immemorial". This change would bring our candidate's
proficiencies closer to those now used in Great Britain and in other Englishspeaking countries abroad.
In returning to our historic proficiencies, we need not lose our current
forms of candidate's lecture. There are many men in California who love memory

Grand Master Doan's Recommendation No. 8
Composition of Junior Grand Warden
Recommending Committee
Many years ago, a system evolved in which Past Grand Masters from the
northern portion of the state and those from the south met separately in alternate
years to recommend a member of Grand Lodge for election as Junior Grand
Warden. After agreement was reached among the Past Grand Masters from both
portions of the state, the name of the recommendee was circulated mouth-to-ear.
In later years, all Past Grand Masters have met collectively to select a
recommend ee alte rnately from the northern and southern portions of the state.
In 1974, these traditions were enacted into law. Provision was made for
written notice of the name and qualifications of the recommendee. Also, three
addit ional men were added to the selection committee, men who would be
appointed by the sitting Grand Master and who would not be past or present elected
Grand Lodge Officers. In 1980, the law was changed again to name the Grand
Master as the chairman of the selection committee, with the power to vote only in
the event of a tie, as is normally the rule in such circumstances.
This process has evolved because of a desire to pursue two goals: to
clarify the rules and to widen the circle of experiences represented at the selection
meeting. The addition of the Grand Master to the selection committee was
particularly important in advancing this second goal. The Grand Master is the one
California Mason un iquely placed to observe the performance and potential of the
possib le candidates for election as Junior Grand Warden.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Deputy Grand Master and the Grand Wardens potentially have much
to contribute to the selection process also. They travel extensively aroWld the state.
~ey sit on the major Boards of Trustees of this Grand Lodge. They meet monthly
with the ~rand Master at Executive Committee meetings. They too have a unique
o~portumty to observe the craft at work. Their observations on occasion may
differ from those of the Grand Master, and those observations would be helpful to
the selection committee.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master Doan recommends that the Deputy Grand Master and Grand
Wardens be included on the Recommending Committee for selection of a
Recommendee for Junior Grand Warden.
The Recommending Committee serves primarily as a Nominating
Committee. The voting delegates to Grand Lodge have the final word.

270

In recognition of this potential, the Deputy Grand Master and Grand
Wardens were invited to attend the selection committee meeting last January.
Because our law does not provide that they are members of the selection
committee, the committee allowed them to attend its deliberations as observers
only. While such observer status could continue in the future, an observer does not
have the same opportunity to contribute that a member has. The participation of
our Deputy Grand Master and Grand Wardens in the selection process cannot reach
its potential unless these men are voting members of the committee.
At the selection committee meeting last January, there were in attendance
twenty-four voting members: twenty-one Past Grand Masters and the three others
appointed by me. The addition of the Deputy Grand Master and Grand Wardens
to this process would not therefore have a significant impact on the result but
would give them the opportunity to contribute to the process with complete candor.
I therefore recommend that they be made part of the process by their addition as
members of the selection committee.
To accomplish that end, I recommend that the first paragraph of Section
510 of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows :
The Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master. the Grand
Wardens. the Past Grand Masters, and three members of Grand
Lodge appointed annually by the Grand Master to serve for a
single term only concurrently with his term and who are not past
or present elected Grand Officers, shall constitute a committee
to recommend to Grand Lodge a member for election as JWtior
Grand Warden. The Grand Master shall call and preside at
meetings of the committee, but shall not vote except in cases of
tie votes. A majority of the whole committee shall constitute a
quorum. A majority vote of those present and eligible to vote
shall be necessary to select the recommendee.

271

Section 510 of the 1993 Masonic Code defines the current procedure
followed by the Grand Lodge of California. Briefly, the Committee to Recommend
to Grand Lodge a Member for Election as Junior Grand Warden consists of all Past
Grand Masters, the Grand Master and three members of Grand Lodge appointed
annually by the Grand Master to serve for a single term only concurrently with his
term and who are not past or present elected Grand Lodge officers.
Please note the last condition with respect to the three members appointed
by the Grand Master. They shall be members "who are not past or present elected
Grand Lodge Officers." Apparently, there was a sound reason for excluding these
officers at the time.
The procedure used by the Grand Lodge of California for decades has
served this Grand Lodge well. It is unique among the Grand Lodges of North
America and other parts of the world. It takes advantage of the accumulated
experience of all living Past Grand Masters which amounts to about l ,000 years.
They have served the Grand Lodge in many different positions culminating in the
prestigious position of Grand Master. The span of experience also covers a period
of nearly half a century, during periods of growth and decline.
There are presently 25 living Past Grand Masters. Usually, the attendance
of Past Grand Masters at the Selection Committee meeting is at least 20. With the
three appointed members, the total attendance is about 23. Only those present have
a vote on the candidates. No absentee votes are cast. The final selection is made
through a process of progressive elimination by secret ballot.
In 1992, an ad-hoc Committee of Past Grand Masters made a study of the
desirability of including the Deputy Grand Master and Grand Wardens as members
of the Selection Committee. This study concluded that it was not necessary for the
Deputy Grand Master and Grand Warden to be present for several reasons.
a.

The Recommending Committee with 28 members from throughout
California is more than adequately staffed to be able to arrive at an
acceptable recommendation.

b.

The Deputy Grand Master and Grand Wardens may suggest names
of prospective recommendees without being physically present at
the meeting.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORN lA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

272

c.

d.

It is not necessary for the Deputy Grand Master to be present to
observe the manner in which the meeting is conducted by the Grand
Master. This has not been a problem for previous Grand Masters.
It is not necessary for these officers to be present in order to learn
the name of the recommend ee, since the selection is not finalized
until the recommen dee agrees to allow his name to be put forward
as the recommend ee. The procedure for announcement of the name
of the recommen dee is defined in Section 510 of the California
Masonic Code.

§33080. LODGE RESTORATION OF SUSPENDED MASON.
A Lodge may, at any Stated Meeting taking place 90 days or more after
the sentence of suspension has been imposed and affinned by Gran<;!
~by the votes of two-thirds of the members present, annul any such

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents o f this Resolution seek to modify and clarify the law in
res pect to reversals of decisions by Grand Lodge and when and how a Mason
suspended after sentence is restored.
If a judgment is reversed, the Resolution defines carefully the responses
by the Lodge, namely prohibiting it from dismissing the charges, but rather to elect
a new Commission and through the offices and functions of the Trial Master to
proceed with the ame nded charges.

In the case of Restoration of a suspended Mason by a Lodge, the new
legislation states that a vote can be taken at a Stated Meeting at least 90 days after

275

the suspension was imposed and affirmed by Grand Lodge. Notice of the vote for
Restoration must be given at the Stated Meeting next preceding the meeting at
which the vote is to be taken.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes finds that the proposed
changes are consistent with present Grand Lodge Policy.

Report of the Committee on Trial Review:
Carry-over Resolution 93-05 makes no substantive change in our law
regarding reversal and restoration after conviction at Masonic Trial, except for a
provision that a suspension must be in effect for 90 days after Grand Lodge has
affirm ed it before a Lodge may annul a suspension and restore the suspended
Mason.
Section 32360 provides that if the penalty is suspension or expulsion "it
shall at once go into effect." To annul a suspension requires the vote of two-thirds
of the Lodge membe rs present at a Stated Meeting.
Though a conviction may be unpopular at the Lodge level, Grand Lodge
may feel strongly enough about it to raise the penalty from suspension to expulsion.
This has happened six times in the past five years. It would be very bad for
everyone involved if a Lodge voted to annul the suspension of a convicted brother
and Grand Lodge later voted to expel him. It is possible that some suspension will
be longer under this Code provision than it might have been without the waiting
period provided, but it will avoid the potential great e mbarrassment to the Lodge
and the accused.
Your Commitfee on Trial Review recommends a "Yes" vote.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

WHEREAS, one of the messages given to prospective Masons is that
Masonry helps to make good men better men through lessons taught in the degrees
and Masonic association; and
WHEREAS, one of the methods o f teaching these lessons is the lectures
given after each degree; and
WHEREAS, the candidates have already been exposed to strange
surroundings and myriad of mental and moral lessons, intended to make them
conscious of the beauty of Masonry, before the lectures, and
WHEREAS, after having been exposed to the aforementioned lessons and
ideas, the candidate is seated in a chair and required to listen to a 20 to 30 minute
lecture given by one man, who at items delivers the lecture in a monotone voice,
that tends to put the sideliners to sleep; and
WHEREAS, it has been proved that the candidates and the sideliners get
more from the lecture when presented by two qualified men. Each man has a
different tone of voice and a different method of delivery which improves the
delivery of the lectures. We have seen the candidates straighten up in their chairs
and listen more intently when the second man starts his section of the lecture.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to restore the requirement that the
Jurisdiction be divided into six divisions. This proposal was prompted by a
substantive change revealed in Section 3030 of the newly-adopted 1991 California
Masonic Code as a result of the Special Committee's revision of Section 1116 of
the 1975 issue of the Masonic Code.
The Special Committee on Code Revision outlined its charge and
guidelines in the preamble of the Resolution as it proceeded and completed its
assignment as follows:
a.

eliminate ambiguities, redundancies, and inconsistencies;

b.

simplify the wording;

c.

reconstitute sections into more logical sequences; and

d.

otherwise restructure the Code without makin2 substantive
chan2es. (Underlining added)

At the time the 1991 Code was adopted the delegates to Grand Lodge
properly assumed that during the revision process it was not the committee's
prerogative to make any changes; that removal of ambiguities, redundancies,
inconsistencies, and simplifying the wording to everyday understandable language
were the main thrust of the undertaking and that it was not the intention of the
Grand Lodge to change the ordinances. Upon review of the results, it now
appears that errors, changes and omissions, unknown to the voting delegates
prevailed at the time of consideration and adoption of the 1991 Code during the
Annual Communication in October of 1992. The main issue addressed in the
carry-over legislation is the concern that the delegates and constituent Lodges were
denied their right to vote on a matter that seriously impacts the efficiency of ritual
administration and has a profound effect on the quality of ritual in this Jurisdiction .
While Grand Master Doan acted within the law, as it was recorded in the
newly-adopted 1991 Masonic Code, in restructuring the several Divisions, none of
the issues concerning monetary savings, whether real or imagined, should be
considered as evidence in this matter. The single issue involved is whether or not
the inadvertent omission of jurisdiction language in Section 3030 of the
California Masonic Code, by the Code Revision Committee, should be
construed as the binding rule. It has been the policy of the Grand Lodge that
such matters in the past ha\'e been of a "housekeeping" nature and were
handled as such. Once the Section has been returned to its original form, then

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

283

new agendas, if any, could be introduced in proper procedure and voted upon
by this Grand Lodge.
Section 810 of the 1991 Code outlines the proper procedure for proposed
amendments to our Ordinances by: (a) presentation of written resolutions by
members of Grand Lodge, (b) decisions and/or recommendations by the Grand
Master, and (c) such emergent matters which may be presented and deemed proper
by the delegates of Grand Lodge. Section 6180 declares that the Committee on
Masonic Code shall edit and prepare for publication the annual changes in our laws
and submit to Grand Lodge any revisions that may seem necessary or desirable.
Your "Yes" vote will restore our Jurisdiction into Divisions as they existed
prior to the adoption of the 1991 Code; whereas, a "No" vote will retain the law as
it now exists in Section 3030 in the new version of the Code.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Neither a Lodge, a Masonic Organization, nor a Mason shall; directly~
indireetl~·, gi.,·e er eMempt te gi·, e the eid er eettntenllftee ef Mft:'len."")' te,
6t' participate in; the conduct or preparation of any raffle, lottery, bingo
game or other gambling enterprise, conducted in the name of, or directly
er direetl)' for the monetary benefit of; any Lodge or of any Masonic

Report ofthe Committee on Po/icy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this resolution seek to remove certain restrictions
covering gambling as currently legislated in Section 15090 of the California
Masonic Code to allow Temple Associations to rent their buildings to nonmasonic
organizations for the purpose of hosting games of change when there are no cash
prizes and the gaming events do not violate state and local laws.
The issue of legislating gambling has been the subject of debates in this
Grand Lodge on numerous occasions in the past. The law as it exists today is
basically the same statute that was adopted in 1936 when Grand Master Earl
Warren, in a very logical and impressive way, called the attention of Grand Lodge
to a vice or abuse that had disturbed our Grand Jurisdiction for a number of years.
It had to do with the roatter of gambling by Master Masons who were attached to
or connected with or acting for other organizations. The question of the time most
seriously discussed and one in which there was absolute unanimity of opinion, was
the growing evil of lotteries and other gambling enterprises sponsored by Master
Masons to secure funds for the use of organizations collateral to Masonry.
While the conduct of these illegal enterprises was declared to be
unmasonic conduct, this rule of Grand Lodge was honored in breach more than in
observance by the Master Masons in our Jurisdiction. By admission of the Grand
Master no defmite action had been taken by Grand Lodge or Grand Masters in the
past to enforce the then-existing weak anti-gambling regulations. It appeared when
an illegal gambling enterprise was engaged in, that hundreds of Master Masons
were induced to Jay themselves open to Masonic trial. Accordingly, the Grand
Master recommended that Grand Lodge adopt a definite policy on the subject of
gambling and enact legislation which would insure its effectiveness. Thus the evil
would be remedied and no brother would be injured. This brought about the policy

290

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

and legislation which exists today.
Section 326.5 of the California Penal Code permits only Bingo games to
be conducted in those cities and counties which have adopted ordinances allowing
Bingo to be played. It also provides that Bingo games must be open to the general
public. Our Masonic Law, and consequently our policy, does not allow the use of
Masonic premises to conduct public or private gambling enterprises. Section 326.5
of the Penal Code also requires that any bingo games must be conducted by a nonprofit, charitable organization on property owned or leased by it and used as its
office or to conduct its activities.
Section 330 of the California Penal Code covers the broader subject of
gambling. If we were to remove the restrictions to gambling to permit additional
games of chance as proposed in Resolution 94-04, it is conceivable that infractions
covering lotteries, gaming devices, punchboards, cards, dice, etc. could unfold over
a period of time and restore the dilemma which existed prior to 1936.
Assuming that Bingo would be the chosen game of chance by the
sponsoring body, it would be permitted only in those cities and counties in
California which have enacted ordinances permitting the playing of Bingo. A great
many have not. ln those areas which have approved the playing of Bingo, there are
strict and sometimes costly licensing requirements. In addition there are often
limitations as to the number of licenses which can be issued.
Adoption of this Resolution would therefore, permit the game of chance
in only a limited number of our Masonic Temples. Since ordinances permitting the
event vary from one area to another and since any violation of the State laws
constitutes a misdemeanor, Temple Associations undertaking this activity would
have to exercise extreme caution. Guidance from Grand Lodge in this matter
would not be possible, or at least be very limited, because of the different
requirements in each community.
Our Temple facilities traditionally are available to our Youth Groups for
their meeting places. Gambling enterprises would not be in good taste ifthe events
should take place during the meeting time of these groups. During 1989
considerable tension resulted between the Grand Master and a Chapter Dad who
was the proponent of a DeMolay Casino Night to be held in a Masonic facility.
Relaxation of our gambling laws could conceivably revive such activities.
Adoption of this Resolution would represent a significant change in Grand
Lodge policy. It would in some instances approve a form of legalized gambling
in our Temples . Because of the limitations imposed by State and Local laws it
would extend this approval to a limited number of Lodges and Temple
Associations in this Jurisdiction. This is not in keeping with the Grand Lodge

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

291

Policy of equal treatment of all Masons and Masonic Organizations and cou Id be
construed special interest legislation where one group of members would have
privileges that are not shared by others.

Report ofthe Committee on Finance:
Resolution 94-04 permits Masonic Temple to rent to organizations
conducting lawful games of chance. If this resolution is adopted, your Committee
on Finance finds no effect on Grand Lodge finances.

The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit the use of a copy of a dues receipt
as well as the original dues receipt when applying for affiliation.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the first sentence of each
of paragraphs A and D of Section 26050 of the California Masonic Code be
amended to read:
A.

If the applicant be a member in good standing in this Jurisdiction,
a receipt or a copy of a receipt from the Lodge of which he is a
member showing that his dues are paid through at least the current
calendar year together with a written request, signed by him, to his
Lodge for a Dimit, except as provided for herein.

D.

If the applicant is a member in good standing in this Jurisdiction and
desires to hold plural membership, a receipt or a copy of a receipt
from the Lodge of which he is a member showing his dues are paid
through the current calendar year.

.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution apparently are concerned that a member
applying for affiliation or plural membership must surrender his dues receipt which
must accompany his application.
They propose to eliminate this requirement by adding words which would
permit a copy of the dues receipt to be used rather than the original.
Section 14010 already provides that "whenever this Section requires a
dues receipt be presented, a photocopy thereof, duly certified by the Secretary of
the Lodge, may be substituted.
The precedent for the use of a photocopy has therefore been established,
and is therefore considered to be adequate for a member applying for affiliation or
plural membership.

Resolution 94-09
Eliminates Investigation of Applicants for Arfiliation
The proponents of this Resolution seek to eliminate investigations of applicants for
affiliation unless an objection is made by a Brother.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, we submit this resolution with the firm belief that it is a
change long over due; and
WHEREAS, when an applicant first applies to take the degrees of
Masonry a full and extensive investigation is conducted on his character and
background; and
WHEREAS, any behavior or conduct that would render him unfit for
membership in any Lodge would be reflected on the Certificate of Standing
accompanying his application; and
WHEREAS, in the rare event that an applicant who is not in good standing
manages to become elected, when such comes to light, said applicant would be
subject to charges of un-Masonic conduct and expulsion from the Fraternity; and
WHEREAS, this Resolution will, we hope, impart a more favorable
atmosphere of Fraternal trust and therefore encourage members to affiliate with
Lodges sooner when they move to a new area.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLV ED that the first paragraph of
Section 26120 be amended as follows:
All applications for the degrees ftl'Hl fer 1tff11i1ttie" shall be
referred to a committee of three, unless dispensation has been
granted by the Grand Master to receive them without reference
to a committee. The members of the Investigating Committee
and its report shall be known only to the Master. It shall be the
duty of the committee to make strict examination into the moral,
mental, physical and other proper qualifications of the applicant,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

299

and to report to the Master at the next Stated Meeting, unless he
grants further time. The Investigating Committee shall inform
themselves as to the character of the applicant. They are guilty
of a serious neglect of duty if they report favorably on an
application without reliable information as to all matters on
which the Lodge requires advice. Any apolication for affiliation
will be voted on with no requirement for jnvestieation ynless an
investieation is requested by a Brother. in which case the
application shall be referred to an investieatine committee as
herein provided for.

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend Section 26120 by
eliminating the requirement for investigations of Masons applying for affiliation.
At the present time it is required that all applications to a Lodge, whether they be
for membership or affiliation, be referred to a committee for such investigation.
The proponents argue that applicants seeking affiliation have already
undergone an extensive investigation and that a second such inquiry is superfluous.
This may not always be the case. Certainly not all Masons remain true to their
obligations, as evidenced by occasional instances in which charges ofunmasonic
conduct are upheld. To a lesser degree, a man may engage in questionable
behavior and still maintain good standing in his Lodge, especially if he does not
regularly associate with his brethren but continues to pay his dues. Should such a
man then choose to join another Lodge, this information would only become
available through the inVestigative process. In fact, the absence of an investigative
process might be an inducement for such men to seek affiliation with California
Lodges.
The investigation, if accomplished in the applicant's home, may also serve
to familiarize the applicant's wife, and perhaps even children, with Masonry and
the new lodge to which affiliation is being sought.
The resolution is not consistent with the policy of Grand Lodge.
Resolution CARRIED-OVER.

Resolution 94-10
Modifies Installation Service to Allow
For Joint Installations
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend the Installation Service to allow
for the joint installation of Lodge officers.
To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F.& A.M of California:

WHEREAS, it is the Master's duty to provide for the installation of his
successor in the manner prescribed by Grand Lodge; and
WHEREAS, it may be the Master's desire to hold a joint installation with
another Lodge for fraternal, financial or civic reasons; and
WHEREAS, there is no definitive prohibition of joint installations in the
Masonic Code; and
WHEREAS, there exists a ninety-four year history of continuous joint
installations recorded in minute books with the Grand Master of Masons in
California presiding as Installing Officer for twenty-five of those years, the Grand
Lecturer presiding as Installing Officer for two of those years, other Grand Lodge
Officers presiding as Installing Officer for nineteen of those years and the Grand
Lecturer acting as Master of Ceremonies for nineteen of those years; and
WHEREAS, the current installation service is written for a single Lodge
only; and
WHEREAS, the installation service has been altered through revisions in
the past; and
WHEREAS, the current Ritual Committee has failed to see the merit of
allowing exemptions for joint installation requests.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that two Lodges may
participate in a joint installation of officers and that the Installation Service be
amended to provide for said joint installation, as follows : (1) the instructions shall
pennit singular words be made plural when circumstances require, (2) where one
Lodge is currently identified by name, both Lodges shall be identified, (3) the line
of march for a joint installation shall provide for the Master of Ceremonies to walk
between the Tilers with the officers of each Lodge following single file behind their
respective Tiler, (4) the officers of one Lodge shall be seated on one leg of the "V"
facing their counterparts on the other leg, and (5) the Installing Officer shall install
the officers from both Lodges concurrently for each chair.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

JOI

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Section 25120 of the California
Masonic Code be amended as marked:

§25120. INSTALLATION.
The officers, including incumbents, shall be installed in the manner
prescribed by Grand Lodge, as soon as practical after their election or
appointment, and shall hold their respective offices until their successors
have been duly elected or appointed and installed .
The installation may be performed by the Master or, by invitation of the
Master, by any qualified Past Master of any jurisdiction. It is not the
privilege of the Master-elect to select the Installing Officer or in any way
interfere with the duties and privileges of the office of Master. If
perfonned by a Past Master, the Master or a Warden of the Lodge must
be present. There can be no installation by proxy. Installation may be
private or public. Two Lodees may participate in a joint installation.
The Certificates required for installation, endorsed by the Installing
Officer, shall be forwarded to the Grand Secretary.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend the California Masonic
Code and the Installation Service to allow for the joint installation of Lodge
Officers from two Lodges. This amendment would codify fonnally a practice that
has existed between two Lodges for 94 years.
As currently written, the California Masonic Code calls for the installation
of officers "in the manner prescribed by Grand Lodge." The official Installation
Service is clearly written in the singular, implying that that "manner" is intended
to be for a "one Lodge" installation.
However, it must be noted that, on numerous occasions, these joint
installations have been presided over by a sitting Grand Master, acting as the
Installing Officer. The fact that a Grand Master was the Installing Officer at such
an installation implies that joint installations are acceptable practices.
Throughout the jurisdiction, each of the individual Lodges has developed
its own unique traditions. In fact, these traditions are often responsible for a
particular member developing a sense of loyalty and personal involvement in his
own Lodge. As long as these traditions are consistent with Grand Lodge policy and
procedures, Grand Lodge has not insisted that they be abandoned. It would

Report ofthe Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Most Worshipful, Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
The purpose of this Resolution is very simple. It is to correct an error
introduced into the Proceedings of the 1992 Annual Communication.
The Proceedings of the Grand Lodge, as in any organization, are a true
and faithful record of the transactions of that organization; recorded in printed form
exactly as the business was transacted. Furthermore, it is the duty of the Secretary
(in the case of the Grand Lodge, the Grand Secretary) to attest to the accuracy of
the Proceedings. After the completion of the business, no changes in the record are
permissible, except by a vote of the constituents.
For those who are not familiar with the history of this Resolution, a brief

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

report on the background may be helpful. In 1991, Grand Master Sherod
recommended that Masonic Lodges be allowed to advertise in accordance with a
set of rules spelled out in the recommendation. It was intended that the "other
Masonic organizations be free to develop their own rules on advertising. When the
recommendation was presented to Grand Lodge of a vote, the legislative language
included "other Masonic organizations in the same set of rules. This was consistent
with the Policy and General Purposes of the Grand Lodge that all Masonic groups
be treated alike. It is not uncommon for a Grand Master's Recommendation to be
modified before being presented for a vote and, to the best recollection of those
Committee members involved, such modification was made with the concurrence
of Grand Master Sherod.

footnote on page 225 of the 1992 Proceedings to ensure that .the .Proceedings are
a complete and accurate account of the Annual Commumcat10n and that no
alteration is pennitted in any Proceedings.

306

The measure did not receive a five-sixths vote for adoption and was
carried over to 1992 when it was adopted by a two-thirds vote. A new Code was
adopted in 1991 to become effective at the close of the Annual Communication in
1992.
After the close of the 1992 Annual Communication, it was discovered that
some inconsistencies existed in two versions of the language of the
recommendation that was distributed to the Lodges during 1992. One version bore
the old Code number and the other, the new Code number. The one with the old
Code number expressed the original intent of Grand Master Sherod. The other
contained the language presented to the delegates for vote in 1991 and again in
1992. The 1992 Proceedings included both versions, but the printing of the
Proceedings was held up pending a resolution of the inconsistency.
During 1993, after many meetings on the subject, Grand Master Doan
decided that Grand Master Sherod's original intentions should prevail and ordered
the insertion of a footnote in the 1992 Proceedings to reflect that decision. Many
brethren in leadership roles in the Grand Lodge did not agree with that decision
because of the finn belief that the delegates were fully aware that they had voted
on the legislation that included "other Masonic organizations."
In a compromise agreement with the Committee on Jurisprudence, Grand
Master Doan presented his decision for ratification by the delegates by a majority
vote {which is a highly irregular procedure). The delegates voted in favor of the
decision. As the matter now stands, only Masonic Lodges are governed by the
advertising regulations.
The adoption of this Resolution will not change the advertising legislation
in
adopted 1993. If any change is desired, it must be done through the recognized
procedure of submitting Resolutions.
Your affmnative vote will do nothing more than eliminate or correct the

Resolution ADOPTED.

PROCEEDINGS OF Tl IE

We are continuing the policy established by Most Worshipful Blomseth
during his year as Foundation president by assigning a trustee to each of the
individual scholarship funds. Each fund representative is knowledgeable regarding
donor stipulations, current condition of the fund including corpus and scholarships
issued, maintains contact with the donor and reports ast least quarterly to the Board
of Trustees.
It was our pleasure to fund 78 scholarships for the 1994/1995 school year.
Of these, 25 were renewals and 53 were new awards.
We also moved our application deadline back to February 28th of each
year in order to complete the selection process and have scholarships ready for
presentation at high school award ceremonies. This change should increase public
awareness of our Fraternity and ensure the students receive their awards before
leaving for college.
The deadline for renewing students was moved back to February 1st
which allows us to review their applications and provide funding before accepting
new applications.
The concept of living trusts has created a major source of potential future
funds for the Foundation. During this current year the Foundation received such
a trust from Ted and Ruby Wade. They were great supporters of our youth and the
Order of Amaranth and gave their estate, consisting of three mutual funds and an
apartment complex, to the Foundation to establish the Wilson 0. "Ted" and Ruby
S. Wade Amaranth Scholarship Fund. This fund totals $763,205 as a result of the
sale of the apartment complex and the liquidation of the mutual funds.
Brother Victor Carver, a member of Poinsettia Lodge No. 633, left his
estate to the California Masonic Foundation. At the present time this estate is in
probate court and should be received by the Foundation by year end 1994. It is
anticipated the estate will be in excess of $800,000 after court mandated costs.
Together with the Wade estate, the receipt of these funds will substantially
increase the Foundation's resources and the magnitude of the scholarship program.
The popularity of the school box program faded during the past couple of
years. Therefore, no additional funds were expended during the current Grand
Lodge year as the supply on hand was adequate for our needs. Most Worshipful
Blomseth presented boxes at several cornerstone ceremonies and many lodges
presented them during programs emphasizing our support of the public school
system. The Foundation will continue to oversee this program until the present
supply of approximately 24,000 boxes is exhausted.

presents its 102nd Annual Report of the Masonic Homes of California for the fiscal
year July l , 1993 through June 30, 1994.

The Board of Trustees met in San Francisco, California on October 14,
1993, for the purpose of organization. The election of William F. Stovall (540),
Deputy Grand Master; Charles H. Alexander (111), Senior Grand Warden; and
Allen B. Gresham (348), Junior Grand Warden, was fonnally reported to the Board
and pursuant tot he provisions of the California Masonic Code, they became
members of the Board, ex-officio. In addition to the Grand Lodge Officers, the
Board was composed of the following Trustees for tenns as of the close of the

Board Meetings
Meetings of the Trustees are usually held on the first Wednesday of the
month, alternating between the Union City and Covina Homes.
Committees of the Board usually meet the day before Board meetings to
review or prepare reports for Board consideration.
You will note that the Administrators and members of the Board of
Trustees have been given the opportunity to participate in the preparation of this
Annual Report as follows:
Admissions Committee

by Victor Howard, Ph.D., and Ernest A. Pooleon, Co-Chairmen
The Admissions Committee of the Board of Trustees meets on the first
Tuesday. of each month. This infonnal meeting allows for a free exchange of
information about each of the applicants between the Trustees of the north and the
south and the Homes Administrators, Representatives and Medical staff.
Prior to the Tuesday meeting, the eight Trustees who fonn the Admissions
Committee (four from the North and four from the South) have received and
carefully studied the aplications for prospective residents and/or nonresident
assistance. These Trustees evaluate the applications and pass their comments and

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

votes to the two co-chairmen. The co-chairman in charge for that month (the cochainnen alternate responsibility) then produces a preliminary Admissions
Committee Report.
Following the Tuesday Admissions Committee Meetng and the input
received from the medical staff at the Home, this Preliminary Admissions
Committee Report may be modified to reflect the discussions. The revised
Admissions Committee Report is then presented to the full Board of Trustees at the
formal Board Meeting on Wednesday, where the final decisions is made on each
appl ication.
The number of applications handled by the Committee for couples,
individuals and children varies from month to month. This past year the high was
8 applications handled in one month for seniors, and 6 aplications in one month for
children.
Because of the need to control admissions as we entered a period of
reconstruction of the Union City facility, and because the Skilled Nursing Facility
was operating close to maximum capacity, the number of persons admitted to
Assisted Living was significantly decreased during the year. During the last
quarter of the year, as the process of reconstruction was begun, another consequent
need to move residents from one area of the Home to another, admissions were
restricted to those classified as "Independent Ambulatory." As was anticipated, this
has resulted in an increase in the number of persons being assisted through
Nonresident Assistance (NRA).

The co-chairmen gratefully acknowledge the hard work and dedication of
the Trustees who are on the Admissions Committee. The members are Warren
Buschmann, Charles Alexander, Arthur Triebel, Allen B. Gresham, and Frederick
L. Sorsabla. We also acknowledge the work of the two Administrators, John Rose
and Kelly Wiest, and their excellent staff.

320

Paralleling this reduction at Union City, the number of residents in the
adult section of Covina was increased to its maximum capacity, although at present
we continue to be limited in the level of applicants we can accept by the lack of onsite medical and nursing facilities.
During the latter part of this year, we have re-opened another cottage for
children at Covina as a result of a significant number of new admissions.
The co-chairmen sincerely thank the other Trustee members of the
Admissions Committee who labor long and hard over these applications. All
Trustees try to make a thoughtful judgement for what is best for the applicants
within the capabilities available within our facilities.
Excellent support and dedication to the applicants and Trustees is
provided by Karla Griffin, Homes Representative-North, and Carolyn Tolcher,
Homes Representative-South; and Kira Reginato, Director of Outreach Services.
Kitty Teal and Ron Bunty of Covina also assisted in the South.

Personnel Committee

by Alvin J. Weis, Chairman
Last year we reported the need for our committee to keep abreast of the
many local, state and federal regulations which govern employee/employer
relations. This led the Board to approve the creation of the new position of
Director of Human Resources.
On January 1, 1994, Dawn Graeff-Barba joined our staff in San Francisco
as the Director of Human Resources. She is directing all aspects of personnel and
"Management Development" at both Homes and in the San Francisco office. Ms.
Graeff-Barba's experience and professional background in personnel in the health
care field is extensive. She and her staff are responsible for overseeing the daily
activities of human resources and our committee can now devote its time and
attention to policy matters and direction.
Priority projects now underway by this committee and staff include
revising and distributing a new "Employees Handbook;" reviewing all job
classifications and developing a comprehensive compensation plan; completion of
the final phase of staff training as required by the "Injury and Illness Prevention
Program." Our goal is to complete these projects during the next fiscal year.

Real Estate Committee

The Board also approved two special programs for two of our young
people involving a special summer camp and a foreign exchange program in

by Stanley M Cazneaux. Chairman
The Real Estate Commitee of the Masonic Homes of California, Board of
Trustees, presently includes the Chairman and one member, Alvin J. Weis.
The Real Estate Committee is charged with the responsibility of disposing
of all real estate made available to the Masonic Homes through asset assignment,
wills and bequests, gifts and grants.
During the past year, July l, 1993 through June 30, 1994, we sold
eighteen (18) pieces of property for a total of $1,539, 175. We sold sixteen {16)
motor vehicles for a total of $24,716, and home furnishings in the amount of
$10,224.32. Total sales for 1993/ 1994 equal $1,574,115.32. In addition,
payments, including payoffs, on our "Notes Receivable" amount to a total of
$874,853.70. We continue to carry forty-two (42) Notes with a total value of
$2, 128, 136. 70.
We always have an inventory of unsold properties, due to the Life Care
Contract signed by each new resident of the Home. This affords them a ninety (90)
day period to adjust and satisfy their own minds that they have no intention of
withdrawing from the Masonic Home. The resident then signs a release
authorizing the sale of the property.
The members of the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of
California wish to express their deep appreciation to Brother Hambleton Leas, Past
President of the Board of Trustees, for his continued assistance in the sale of real
estate. As a consultant to the Real EstatTe Committee, he continues his dedication
to our Masonic Homes.

Planned Giving Program

by Jeff Eichner, Director of Charitable Giving
As we approach the 21st Century the World is rapidly changing and by the
year 2000 - just 5 years from now - California Freemasonry will have changed, too.
There will be fewer members in fewer lodges and the average age of the brethren
will be a lot older.
Since the public is not solicited for funds, Masons are the p~mary support
of the Masonic Homes of California. Charity is woven into the fabnc of Masonry
and through their generosity, Masons have been charitable in their support of the
Homes for more than 100 years.
From 1975 to J993 the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund received more
than $45 m illion in beq~ests, gifts and memorials. In addition, nearly $25 million
in individual contributions were given through the lodges - with the percentage of
donating members generally ranging from 46 percent to 51 percent. In 19?3,
however, the percentage of contributing members dropped to 43 percent. D~r~ng
th is same period individuals also took advantage of the Homes' planned g1vmg
options, i.e., annuity trust, unitrust, and Pooled Income Fund.

by William W. Dickson, Chairman
This year we had three of our graduates from the Home at Covina request
additional funding to continue their education. One young lady just graduated and
is beginning her higher education .
After enjoyable interviews, grants were issued to all four persons based
on their needs.

Planned Giving Options
The Homes' planned giving program offers various gift-making
alternat ives to prospective donors for consideration. This program allows the
opportunity for the donor to plan a gift from current income, from ~ssets, ~r fro~
real estate and, when properly explained, the planned gift can result ma major gift
to the Masonic Homes.

328

PROCEEDrNGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Studies have shown that planned gifts are common for persons over age
65. This is in the Homes favor because 63 percent of the Masons in California are
65 or older. Studies have also shown that, typically, no more than 3 percent of an
organization's constituency will become a planned gift donor. This factor is not in
the Homes favor considering the downward trend of our membership. In 1975
membership was more than 215,000. It is currently about 125,000, with a
projected membership of less than 100,000 before the year 2000.
A financial services firm's 1993 survey showed that only 12.6 percent of
"affluent" Americans knew about charitable gifts of stocks and personal property.
With 7 out of I 0 Americans that die intestate annually there are probably many
"affluent" Masons who do not know the benefits of making such gifts.
A window of opportunity exists for the Masonic Homes to publicize
(more) the advantages of planned giving. The following describes the Homes'
planned giving options and what the Director of Charitable Giving might do to
achieve greater participation by California Masons and their wives and widows in
the planned giving options that can benefit them and benefit the Masone Homes of
California.

In addition to what is being administered by the Masonic Homes, it is
difficult, if not impossible, to determine who has name the Homes in his or her will
or trust unless we are notified. Telephone calls and letters are received monthly
requesting information about how to make planned gifts to the Homes, but in most
cases the details of such gifts are not offered.

participants. As of December 31, 1993 , 64 were still active.

At the end of 1993, the principal of the Pooled Income Fund was nearly
$4 .75 million for the 64 active participants. The principal for individual
participants ranged from $5,000 (9 participants) to $800,000 for one p~icipant.
Sixty-three percent of the participants entered the Pooled Income Fund with a ~ne­
time contribution and never added to the principal, and most of these one-time
contributions were less than $15,000.

There is probably some correlation of the time participants joined the
Pooled Income Fund with ads in the California Freemason. Of the 40 issues from
1984 through 1993, 21 had some kind of publicity about planned giving options
and the Pooled Income Fund was mentioned most often (I 7 times). Although there
were seven new participants in periods when there had been no publicity in three
successive issues ( 1984, 1985 and 1993), the vast majority of new participants got
into the Pooled Income Fund when there was publicity in the California Freemason.

Conclusions and Recommendations
Planned giving options offer a good way for some individuals to make
large donations to the Homes. These options have been successful in the past;
however, there is need for increased participation in planned giving to help in
continuing the vital work of the Masonic Homes. There needs to be an expanded
effort to publicize the Homes' planned giving options and services that can be
provided by the Director of Charitable Giving. The following is recommended for
review and comment.
Goal
Increase the voluntary support from Masons (and their wives and widows)
to continue our commitment to assist needy Masons and their families through the
Masonic Homes of California planned giving options.

Objectives
The key objective in achieving increased participation in the Masonic
Homes' planned giving options is to increase awareness of these opportunities. The
following short-tenn and long-term strategies will hopefully result in an increase
of (I) six new participants in the Pooled Income Fund and (2) six individuals
naming the Masonic Homes of California in their wills or trusts.

REPORT OF THE AnMINISTRA TOR
MASONIC HOME, UNION CITY

Another very special event this year was our Centenarian Birthday Party
in honor of our six residents celebrating I 00+ birthdays. Our two oldest residents,
Ada Hennans from Pasadena Consolidated Lodge No. 272, and Vera Shennan
from Columbia Lodge No. 388 celebrated their 105th birthdays! Mrs. Hennans has
resided here at the Home for the past 32 years. This very happy occasion was
attended by the Mayor of Union City.

1993-1994

As I enter my second year as your Administrator of this great Masonic
Home, I continue to marvel at everything the Masons of California are able to
provide our residents without accepting public funds. The material comforts
provided, environmental maintenance, and medical and nursing care are results of
the untiring efforts of the members of this fraternal order; and it is with this inmind
that I feel privileged to update you on our continual progress and the programs held
during this past year.
Our largest event is the Annual Communication Visitation Day, which
comes closest to bringing all of our lodges together. Our residents look forward to
this yearly event as they can hear, first hand, from their Brothers what is happening
in their respective lodges. Ofour population of303 residents, we have 85 Masons
and 218 spouses and widows, including 26 couples. Our average age is 87. There
are 183 lodges represented at our Home.
I am pleased to report that since our last Annual Communication, 56
Lodges, Eastern Star Chapters, various youth groups and other related groups have
visited and toured the Home.
Our own chartered High 12 Club, #606, which celebrated its 10th
Anniversary on September 28, 1993, continues to hold bi-montly meetings on the
first and third Wednesdays. Support of this club has grown over the years with the
average resident attendance being around 50.
In addition to the above mentioned special events, our residents enjoy
monthly trips to restaurants for lunches and dirrners, to theatrical shows and other
places of interest in the area. Our skilled nursing residents, through dedicated
employee efforts, attend the Shriner's Football Game, Oakland A's baseball games,
and scenic rides.
The second largest and oldest traditional annual event is "Visitation Day
of the East Bay Past Matrons' Association", better known as Jam and Jelly Day.
This event is always held on the third Saturday in August, and 1994 marked its
80th year. Our residents truly enjoy this day, and they are invited to participate in
the program and enjoy the picnic lunch provided by the Association. Annual
donations from this group are used to purchase large print books for our library.
This year, part of the funds were used to purchase computer equipment to be used
by our low vision residents.

333

Over the next five years, we will continue to modernize and improve our
facilities. enhancing the quality of life for our Brothers, their wives and widows.
Most of our buildings housing residents will be remodeled, providing
larger apartments for our residential and assisted living residents. This remodeling
process will include individual controls for heating and air conditioning, improved
TV reception, and the addition of private telephones. At the same time, the Main
Administration Building, North and South Wings, and the Adams Building, will
undergo earthquake retrofit work.
Late last year, the Wollenberg Building was prepared for remodeling, with
construction anticipated to start in the latter part of this year. When completed, it
will house 26 Assisted Living apartments, a new pharmacy, conference room, and
a new area for physcial therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapies; as well
as an exercise area, complete with a spa and hydro-therapy pool.
All renovations are expected to be complete in time for our centennial
year in 1998.
In closing, I wish to express my gratitude to our dedicated, caring
employees who serve our residents, and to the members of the Board of Trustees
and Endowment Board.Members for their conscientious commitment to providing
the best possible services and facilities for the residents .
As residents and employees of this great Masonic Home, we remain
"thankful for all California Masons" for their contributions which make the
Masonic Home for Adults at Union City a great place to live and work.
Respectfully submitted,
Kelly Wiest, Administrator
