It is with pride that I submit this, my fourteenth report to the brethren of
the Grand Lodge of California. This year, my message relates to change within our
·
Masonic Homes at Covina.
Being the Administrator at Covina has been an unusual occupation. In
essence, the manner in which the Masonic Homes of California has evolved over
the last few years has required many of the management team members to be retooled, reeducated, recertified and relicensed in order to be successful in our
mission. For many of us it has been like having several occupations.

Lets discuss the changes at Covina. Organizations, like organisms, must
adapt to their environment in order to survive. The Masonic Homes of California
has survived two world wars, global conflicts, periods of epidemics, the great
depression and we continue to serve effectively in an era of declining family and
social values. In 1985 the Masonic Homes of California began active planning for
the Adult Facility at Covina. By January of 1990 the Adult Home was constructed
and its first 12 residents admitted. The population and service programs have
evolved to the point where we now serve sixty-five adult residents who have
various needs ranging from only basic to significant assistance. At this time the
Board of Trustees is considering a second phase of expansion and deliberating
what, how and by whom will specific adult services be provided.
We serve at 1\ time when "Health Care" is the "sound bite" of the day.
Health Care is more than a sound bite in the Masonic Homes as we provide our
residents the finest health care available. At Covina, we have instituted a managed
care approach to health care for our adult residents and use a host of community
resources which has proved both cost efficient and effective. In this way our
residents have choices relative to their health care and also embrace the
surrounding communities. This use of community resources has reaffirmed that
the Home at Covina remains "Covina's Largest Family" as it has for nearly seventy
years.
The Children's Home is serving at a very difficult time. Since 1898 the
Masonic Home has served orphans. Our Children's Home is older than the foster
care system in California and also the welfare system (Aid To Families With
Dependent Children). Obviously, during the wars, the epidemic periods and the
great depression, we had a larger population of children.

348

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFO RNIA

Social and welfare innovations are a primary reason for the population
decline of children in the Masonic Home. Also, the relationship between the
children and their Masonic sponsor has changed. Nevertheless, there is still a
pressing need in this era of domestic stress. It is not the Master Mason and his wife
who causes domestic stress, violence, substance abuse, neglect or physical abuse
of children. It ii the Master Mason and his wife or widow who is often asked to
help in these situations. Thus, in this phase of our service we see more
grandchildren, nieces and nephews of distressed members of the fraternity or their
wives or widows. Unfortunately, and despite regular publicity in the California
Freemason and lodge presentations, the brethren and their wives remain largely
uninfonned about who can be served in this Children's Home.
Another phase of our evolution is the P.A.L. Program. P.A.L. is an
acronym for Provide A Life. This program of service was made possible by a
portion of the estate of Brother Hennan Tate of Seafaring Lodge, the interest of
which may be used to support the cost of a non-Masonically related child in our
Masonic Home. Application is made as any other, through the constituent lodge.
It is ironic that "Home" Lodge No. 721 has sponsored the first child in our "Home"
under this program. The P.A .L. Trust is endowed and earnings from this fund
supports this specific program alone. The Masonic Homes of California
Endowment Fund continues to support the adults and Masonically related children
under the rules originally laid down by the fraternity. Under the P.A.L. program,
we take our obligation to another level and remember that to relieve the distressed
is a duty incumbent upon all men, particularly Masons!
Organizations, like organisms, seek to survive. As with food and water
to an organism, the fraternity unselfishly provides our essential resources in the
fonn of donations to the Endowment Fund, other contributions and through wills
and estate giving. The Board of Trustees administers these funds and assures the
organization is using these resources in an efficient and effective way.
Organizations, like organisms, convert resources to energy. The energy of the
Masonic Homes of California has always been to relieve distress. Our product
continues to be healthy children prepared spiritually, educationally and culturally
to enter the world. Our product is also those senior citizens in our care who
continue to live their lives to the fullest measure possible. The Masonic Assistance
programs (Masonic Homes at Covina, Union City, Nonresident Assistance and
Outreach Services) will continue to require the support of Masons and their
families during these difficult and trying times.

Thank you for your support and commitment to the Masonic Homes of
California. I count it a pleasure to serve as your Administrator and, during the last
year, to know the following people. Their names represent not only those whom
we love and serve but also tangible evidence of our commitment and obligation as
Masons.

reasons: Worshipful Brothers Douglas Aitken, Robert Bunce and Bruce Johansen.

Bresee, Jr., Joseph Ross, Lauryn Taylor, Herbert Leue, Milburn Cobb, Richard

appointment to this important group.
We have continued the presentation of the book, "The Greatest of These
is Charity," to newly-initiated Entered Apprentice Masons. If your lodge has not
been a part of this program, I urge you to advise your local Homes Endowment
Board Member when First Degrees are planned so that he can ensure the
presentation is made.

The importance of the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund cannot be overemphasized. The fund continues to provide approximately 30% of the total cost
of operating our Homes. With continued increases in costs it is vital that the
Endowment Fund be increased in the same manner. Unfortunately, at the current
pace, we are not keeping up with inflation.

The really unfortunate statistic is that only 43.5% of the Masons in the
Grand Lodge of California made any contribution at all to the Masonic Homes
Endowment Fund. This fact indicates that not enough attention is being paid to
promoting the Masonic Homes within our lodges. Your Endowment board is ready
and willing to assist every lodge in educating the membership to this need. We will
visit your lodge and participate in your programs whenever asked.
I would strongly urge each Master and Secretary to pay close attention to
the letters and telephone calls he receives form his Board member. He should
include the free brochures in many of his trestleboards, publish information on the
Homes, and have at least one major program during the year to promote the
Endowment Fund. Such activities are bound to have significant results.
Brethren, to those of you who have been responsible for the growth in our
fund this past year, and on behaJf of the Masonic Homes of California, I say a very
sincere, "Thank you for your dedication." And, Most Worshipful Grand Master,
on behalf of all of the members of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board, I
likewise thank you for the privilege of serving you, and the Grand Lodge, in this
capacity.
Respectfully submitted,
W. Bruce Pruitt, Chairman

Nob Hill Masonic Management, Inc. ("NHMM'') is a for-profit
corporation wholly owned by the Grand Lodge of California and operates the
phy sical assets of the California Masonic Memorial Temple ("CMMT") as a
general lessee of the temple property located at 1111 California Street, San
Francisco and the adjacent apartment rental properties on Pine Street to the south.
The directors ofNHMM are five in number - four of who are appointed
annually by the Grand Master with the Junior Grand Warden serving as a director
by virtue of his office. Likewise, the Grand Treasurer and the Grand Secretary
serve, respectively, as the Chief Financial Officer and Secretary of the corporation
by vitrue of their offices.
The Board meets on a quarterly basis to consider matters o f policy for the
operation of the corporation under the direction of its Executive Vice
President/General Manager.
On January 13, 1994, an amendment to the by-laws of the corporation was
authorized by the Board and confirmed by the Grand Master in order to conform
the criteria for the appo intment of directors to the reduction in the number of
Masonic Districts.
Also on that date, an amendment to the lease agreement with CMMT was
agreed upon to recognize the need to pay rent based upon net receipts from the
BASS ticket operations and from the parking garage management agreement rather
than based upon gross receipts as provided in the original lease. The amendment
for the parking garage came about because the corporation is no longer paid a net
amount under a lease by the operator and, instead, now receives gross receipts and
pays a ll expenses of operation. The BASS ticket operation was not contemplated
when the lease was originally agreed upon.
On July 14, 1994, a Third Amendment to the by-laws was authorized by
the Board and approved by the Grand Master, clarifying the duties of the President
as the Chief Executive Officer and eliminating the duty of general manager, as that
duty is included with those of the Executive Vice President.
Upon advice of counsel, the management contract with Dakota
Enterprises, Inc. was terminated and, instead, and Employment Agreement was
entered into with Ray W. Ward, C.F.E. Also, the Board authorized the purchase
of key man life insurance insuring the life of its very valuable Executive Vice
President/General Manager, Mr. Ward.

revenue and increased 165% in expense. At the same time, the key indicator,

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON CREDENTIALS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

Your Committee on Credentials is pleased to submit this report of the
registrants at the l45th Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.

The committee is ready to serve any lodge considering consolidation, as
advisors on procedure only. We do not make recommendations as to the items
required to be determined by the lodges consolidating unless there is a conflict with
the California Masonic Code. A Manual for Consolidations is available from the
Chairman of the committee on request and we urge all lodges considering
consolidation to obtain this Manual before proceeding. ln any event, the Chairman
should be contacted to assign a member of the committee to each proposed
consolidation.
We wish to express our thanks to the Grand Master and the Grand Lodge
Office for their assistance whenever requested.
Respectfully submitted,

Budget which covers the period November 1, 1994 to October 31, 1995.
The proposed Budget for the next Grand Lodge year continues the current
level of expenditures with several major differences:

I.

Fraternal expenses will be increased by $10,000.00.

2.

3.

Administration and Grand Lodge expenses will be increased by

$37,000.00.
4.

The Endowment Fund contributions by Grand Lodge is
estimated to be $50,000.00.

5.

Depreciation reserves are estimated to be $44,214.00.

6.

Unfunded expenses (stub period) are reduced by $108,000.00.

7.

Estimated revenue is increased by $34,000.00 including an
expected $25,000.00 dividend from Nob Hill Masonic
Management, Inc.

of California, it would appear that the budgeted expense totals for the fiscal year
ending October 31, 1994 will not be exceeded by the actual dollar amounts spent.

Resolution ADOPTED.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F& A.M of California:

The Investment Committee has the responsibility of reporting annually to
Grand Lodge on the condition of the various funds of Grand Lodge and those
entities.
During the year quarterly meetings are held by the committee with its
invesment counselors. At each meeting an independent analytical consulting firm
reviews the performance of the various funds as compared with similar funds, ie.
Endowment, non-profit and trust funds in the United States.
The primary concern of the committee is the preservation of the principal
of the various funds together with the highest rate of return commensurate with
safety and good investment practice.
Three funds, Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, Masonic Homes General
Fund and the Hugo M. Lorber Union City Fund constitute 91 % of the total
investments.
Among other funds supervised by the committee are the General Fund of
Grand Lodge, the Funds of the California Masonic Memorial Temple, California
Masonic Foundation, Pooled Income, and several restricted-use funds of Masonic
Homes.
The market value of the total portfolio on August 31, 1994 was
$322,202,437.00 compared to $322,593,000.00 a year earlier, a decrease of .01 % .
The approximate 1993-1994 cash yield on the total invested funds was 5.2%

1.22

California Freemason

381

Albert A. fritz
Kenneth E. Miller
Herbert E. Pompey

Fixed income securities, including government and corporate bonds
composed 40% of the total portfolio. The remainder consisted of common stocks
and cash equivalents.
The rewarding accumulation of assets in the various funds of Grand Lodge
has been the result of the efforts of Masons and their friends. The operation of the
Masonic Homes at Union City and Covina are financed almost entirely from the
Endowment and the General Fund investments. The expansion at Union City in
the last several years was funded entirely from the Hugo M. Lorber Fund. Other
revenues furnish support for the charitable activities and educational grants of the
Grand Lodge of California .

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The funds investments rank among the highest in quality because the
Investment Committee exercises the utmost prudence and care in their overseeing
of the management of the funds. During the past year the committee replaced two
of the funds equity managers with three new managers. The cash yield and the
total return have been satisfactory in view of the committees conservative policy
and the securities markets.

Recommendations of the Grand Master may fall into two different
categories. They often times change our Constitution; on such cases a five-sixths
vote is necessary. Where there is no change in our Constitution or Ordinances, a
majority vote only is required for adoption.

The next category of business which will come before you is the "carryover" matters from our 1993 session. Once again these items have been forwarded
to you from the Grand Secretary's office. These are the items on the blue paper,
specifically Grand Master Doan's Recommendations 5, 6 and 8, and the carry-over
Resolutions No. 93-05, 93-06, 93- IO, 93-11 and 93-12. Each of these matters

support but did receive a majority vote. Therefore, under the provisions of our
California Masonic Code, each was automatically carried over for reconsideration.
Carry-over matters such as these require only a two-thirds vote for adoption. Again
in each case the language presented to you is adequate to carry out the intent of the
proponents of the legislation.
Finally the l~t items to be voted upon are the 1994 Resolutions. The
legislative style of presentation used by our Grand Secretary's office makes

you are in a form presented to you for your action by your Committee on
Jurisprudence. In each case a five-sixths vote is required for adoption, except
Resolution 94-12 which does not change our Constitution or Ordinances and
requires only a majority vote.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
MASONIC SERVICE BUREAUS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A.M. ofCalifornia:
The Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus is pleased to submit the
following data as its Annual Report for the Fiscal Year ending June 30, 1994. The
Committee is in its 67th year.
The Committee takes its directive to supervise the operations of the
several Masonic Service Bureaus in the State of California very seriously. These
Bureaus, which number 13, extend from the San Diego in the South, to Sacramento
in the North, assist in rendering Relief to Distressed Worthy Brothers and their
families residing in the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge F & AM of California.
Sojourners as well as California Masons receive assistance when the situation
requires it. The Committee also assists the Masonic Service Association in the
continuing development of its "Hospital Visitation Program" at several of the
Veterans Administration Facilities in California. Members of the Committee in
conjunction with Executive Secretaries of the. Bureaus also participate in the work
of the Masonic Relief Association of the United States and Canada.

There are several new Executive Secretaries since the previous years
the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A .M. of California. The San

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON PRINCE HALL RECOGNITION STUDY

To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F&AM of California:
This special committee was formed in October 1990 at the direction of the
Grand Master as a result of a verbal agreement between the incoming Grand Master
and the proponent of Resolution 90-07, calling for the recognition of Prince Hall
Masonry, when it was withdrawn from consideration before the 1990 Annual
Communication.
The original purpose of the committee was stated as:

1.

To study the future relationship between the Grand Lodge of California
and the M.W. Prince Hall Grand Lodge F&AM State of California, Inc.
and their constituent lodges;

2.

To meet with representatives of the M. W. Prince Hall Grand Lodge
F&AM State of California, Inc. , and

3.

To report to the 1991 Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of
California its Findings.

After delivering that report at the 1991 Annual Communication of our
Grand Lodge ,and again in 1992 and 1993, recommendations were adopted that
your special committee be continued for the ensuing Masonic Year, as presently
composed, with an explicit charge to bring before the next Annual Communication
its proposals and recommendations respecting some form of recognition of the
M. W. Prince Hall Grand Lodge F&AM State of California, Inc. and also that the
Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master and their designees continue to meet
informally with corresponding representatives of the M. W. Prince Hall Grand
Lodge F&AM State of California, Inc. Having sought your approval before acting,

Since shortly after our formation as a committee we have met with a like
committee from the M. W. Prince Hall Grand Lodge F&AM State of California,
Inc. After our initial request for these meetings, the formally arranged meetings
have been supplemented by informal meetings and conversations between
individual members of both committees. We continue to distribute our formal
meeting minutes as a joint committee. With each meeting the joint committee
obtains a better understanding of the other's fraternal culture and the meaning and
importance of words being used in our discussions.
This special committee has met twice over the past Masonic Year during
the months of March and June with the similar committee of the M. W. Prince Hall
Grand Lodge F&AM State of California, Inc. Through all our deliberations we
continue to be impressed with the quality, depth, and sincerity of the commitment
of these men representing Prince Hall Masonry. We operated to carry out the
recommendations of the past Annual Communication. Additionally, prior to this
1994 Annual Communication, Deputy Grand Master William Stovall attended the
July Grand Sessions of Prince Hall as their invited guest representing the Grand
Master. He was afforded two opportunities to address the membership and their
ladies. Each event visit and talk was well received.
At our 1993 Annual Communication, your special committee dealt with
the basic steps of the recognition process. We have been convinced by the study,
time, and events that the origin of Prince Hall Masonry was regular and has
remained so. At the 1993' Annual Communication the application of the American
Doctrine of Territorial Jurisdiction to this Grand Lodge was reviewed and decided
by our Grand Lodge. The traditional and historic relations with non-recognized
Masons have been reviewed and clarified. We have changed our methods of
socially relating to non-recognized Masons.
Our Grand Lodge has taken steps which are reasonable to take toward
recognition. Each step we proposed did not require concurrence from Prince Hall.
Each step to this point was to seek the hannony of our present actions and the
existing desires of our Brethren. Now your special committee has come to that
point where each step must be concurrent with similar acffvity of the M. W. Prince
Hall Grand Lodge.
During the past year the joint committee had two formal meetings. We
have discussed how future steps might be taken. At their July '94 Grand Session,
the M.W. Prince Hall Grand Lodge adopted its committee's report to "pursue the
development of legislation on the question of mutual " visitation" for possible

390

PROCEEDfNGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

adoption by the MWPHGL in July 1995." We have come to that point in time
where there is a clear vision of how to proceed. Future efforts with regard to Prince
Hall will be directed at limited recognition within our present CMC definition of
Recognition (refer to CMC 220 ). Such a request for recognition for "visitation"
purposes would place the request on a par with 7 of the 8 Grand Lodges that have
granted visitation. The request through the M.W. Prince Hall Grand Lodge report
set forth the required steps needed to be taken by your special committee . While
we consider the process of recognition, it is well to focus on its broader purpose.
From the Prince Hall report, "Having fraternal relations with, and providing rights
of visitation between the California Grand Lodge and the M. W. Prince Hall Grand
Lodge of California, will not impair the integrity or the supremacy of either
jurisdiction". And while we think of our changes, we must remember that Prince
Hall too has its own Masonic Code which it can not violate.

Additionally we must remember the Master of the individual lodge has the
obligation ( and right ) to control all the visitors and preserve the general harmony
of his lodge which is very dependent on local events. The key to a successful
visitation is mutual respect. The comfort of the visitor, and also the host, lies in the
coordination ahead of the visit which makes it compatible with everyone's plans.

To this the California Grand Lodge members might ask " where are we
going then"? It is clear there are three (3) steps we need to take toward
implementing the favor of visitation if you vote positively.
First, a change is needed in the CMC allowing visitation because the only
current acceptable form today is complete affiliation. The CMC change has to be
approved by the time a joint resolution is approved. The second step, a joint
resolution with exact wording and intent between the two Grand Lodges must be
developed and ratified by each Grand Lodge. The timing for ratification is not an
issue. At present we anticipate any ratification would be performed at the Annual
Communication as regular business rather than at a special session timed to be
coincident with the other Grand Lodge. Prince Hall meets annually in July, three
(3) months prior to ours. The third step is a complete letter of understanding setting
out the details of how a "visitation" takes place. As with the two previous steps the
members of Grand Lodge can make comments to us about how this should occur.
We should focus on "what is" and "what is not" visitation. Since October
'93, social interaction has been allowed and described by the Grand Master' s
Decision No. 6 and by CMC appendix of the Grand Master's interpretative
decisions. The subject of "what is" visitation would cover the esoteric portions and
would allow attending in a tiled lodge. Visitation would allow each Grand Lodge' s
members the favor to visK tiled meetings ( which are presently prohibited ). While
providing such a favor, it is well for our members to remember this is much like
visiting the "home" of a friend. You might drop-in unannounced if you visit such
a friend frequently. But you may remember the tentative nature of your initial visits
and that you felt the need to call ahead until everyone was comfortable. Visiting a
friend's home deals with one's general deportment and not a section of the CMC.

391

Let us take a moment to direct our attention to "what is" and "what is not"
visitation and "who" is allowed to visit. Without setting specifics, the mechanics
of the actual visitation has worked easily in other jurisdictions. The specifics are
centered on possession of(l) a current signed dues card, (2) supported by a list of
approved lodges, and (3) conducting an established test oath. Such a visitation
starts with concurrence of each Grand Lodge's Grand Lecturer. There is less
complexity in the process than one might expect. The process is not open to all
Masons. There are current restrictions on Prince Hall Masons. From Section 22 of
their Constitution, "No (Prince Hall) Mason shall be a Member of more than one
Lodge at a time". The future visitation will involve a finite list of lodges and their
members. Prince Hall Masons have a 6 month grace period to join a local lodge if
they relocate, and they are without a grace period for an "out-of-date" dues card.
Our CMC Sections 2401 O and 24020 show that the Master controls all visitation.
Within the future actions your special committee might propose relating
to the visitation favor, those future actions will apply to lodges under the M. W.
Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California, Inc. jurisdiction only. Other Prince Hall
Grand Lodges, and especially including those Prince Hall jurisdictions recognized
by other Grand Lodges, are not part of this recognition process. Also those tenned
" non-Prince Hall" lodges are not a part of this recognition process. For members
of other Grand Lodges we recognize who reside in or visit in California, but who
do not possess dual membership in our Grand Lodge, they would not be extended
the favor of visiting a Prince Hall lodge by any action we propose.
As we approach the continuation of our activity during the forthcoming
Grand Lodge Year, your special committee seeks to have Grand Lodge confinn our
plans for the 1994/95 Masonic Year. The joint committee has agreed to work with
the following general outline:
A.

To seek additional opportunities to join in public ceremonies with a target
of one cooperative cornerstone ceremony.

B.

To inform the Brethren, the Prince Hall Deputy Grand Master spoke at the
October 9th Open Public Ceremony of our 1994 Annual Communication
and attended the Vespers Service. Tonight the Deputy Grand Master will
be the guest of the Grand Master at the Monday Gala Dinner and Dance.

Ceremony.

Through our Executive Committee, to invite the Prince Hall Grand

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

The charter for the Grand Lodge Committee on Public Schools is found in
Section 6060 of the C.M.C. and reads as follows, "The Committee on Public
Schools shall develop and promote methods of increasing interest in and support
for the Public Schools." The activities and achievements outlined in the following
report are founded on these 20 words.

Packets for Senior Wardens
We started our year at the October 1993 Annual Communication of Grand
Lodge by making sure that the Senior Wardens (who were to be Masters during the
following calendar year) were supplied with the necessary information and
materials to get them started on preparations for their Public Schools Observance
in April. Packets of printed and other materials were assembled by members of our
committee on the Saturday prior to the opening of Grand Lodge. The many
successful Observances that follow justify these procedures.

395

Public Schools Month
By far the most important event of the school year is the annual observance of
Pub lic Schools Month in April. To promote this affair, all committee members
were assigned to lodges in their areas with instructions to contact them at their
District meetings. Essentially these meetings were pep rallies at which the
committeemen displayed their promotional material and, while so doing, instructed
the lodges how to make use of the material to promote successful Observances.
The results were highly satisfactory .
Meetings
Two meetings were convened by our committee during 1993/ 1994. The first
was January 16, and the second was May 22. They were highly productive. A
fringe benefit of such meetings are that they unify our committee. We came away
with an awareness of what other members have done, are doing and what they will
do in the future. Another benefit is a feeling that none ofus work in a vacuum; we
are a cooperative group.
School Boxes
Our committee has been asked by the Masonic Foundation and the Executive
Committee to take on the responsibility for the distribution of school boxes. Of
course, we readily agreed. Each box contains a pencil, an eraser, a ruler and
crayons. As part of our drug abuse prevention program there is a prominent
warning on each box: "DRUGS ARE FOR LOSERS ." Although these boxes are
distributed free to elementary school children at cornerstone laying ceremonies, our
committee urges lodges to buy them at $1.50 per box and distribute them to pupils
in elementary schools in their areas. To encourage lodges to participate in this
endeavor, the members of our committee are, at this time, contacting them at
District meetings throughout the state to impress upon them the importance of this
project. Each lodge will receive I box to allow the brethren of his lodge to be
aware of the school box program and urges them to participate in this program.
Little Red School House Pins
Another give-away item that has met with enthusiastic reception by our lodges
is the Little Red School House lapel pin. In view of their popularity we have urged
th e lodges to purchase them in quantities at $1.25 each, for distribution to those
attending Public School Week Observances and other Masonic gatherings. When
wom by members of our Craft, the message is clear: "The Masons are strong

396

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

supporters of the Public Schools!"
The "Choice" Initiative
On November 2, I 993, the voters of California made a monumental decision.
On that date they went to the polls and cast their ballots against ... the California
Constitutional Amendment called the "Parental Choice in Education Initiative"
(Proposition 174).
In the Autumn 1993 issue of the California Freemason, our Grand Master, R.
Stephen Doan (featured in the centerfold), wrote a detailed critique of the measure.
The Public Schools Committee provided each Master Mason, Inspector, and Grand
Lodge Officer of California information regarding the pros and cons of this
pending proposition. In addition, two thousand copies were distributed among
public schools and the citizenry thereby allowing the citizenry to make an
education choice.
Pipeline to the Senate
Our committee is fortunate in having a direct contact with the California State
Legislature, Senator Ralph Dills, a member of our fraternity who is also a Jong-time
member of our committee. His interest in and support for our Public Schools is
well know. Because of this interest and support we are kept informed of all
pending legislation whose passage would affect our schools.
His most recent contribution to our committee and to the welfare of our Public
Schools was his diagnosis and critique of the "Parental Choice in Education
Initiative" on which the voters casted their ballots. Senator Dills' input is always
valuable.
Proclamations
We have long been aware of the publicity value of Public Schools Month
Proclamations. This year, as in all previous years, we urged lodges to obtain such
proclamations from local city and county officials. Our committee set a good
example by obtaining similar proclamations from the state governor and the state
legislature. In addition, we drafted a proclamation for our Deputy Grand Master
to use as his Public Schools Week Proclamation during his year as Grand Master
in 1995. After editing, it was accepted.

397

Pamphlets
This year we printed 10,000 pamphlets extolling the achievements of our
Public Schools and expressing Masonry's interest in their welfare. Although these
pamphlets were intended for distribution throughout the year, they were especially
effective at Public Schools Month Observances, Public School Cornerstone
Ceremonies, or used as part of table settings at dinner meetings.
Fillers
Many Master have difficulty in filling out their lodge bulletins. As a service
to these Masters we supplied them with what we call "fillers" to fill in the gaps in
their trestleboards. These fillers contain interesting information about Public
Schools and were written with the Master in mind. It is pleasing to note that many
Masters used them as part ... or all ... of their Master's Message.
Jackets, Shirts and Hats
We are always on the lookout for new ways to "develop and promote
methonds of increasing interest in and support for Public Schools." To this end we
laid in a supply of white jackets, white shirts, and white hats, each bearing the Little
Red School House and the message in bold letters: "SUPPORT PUBLIC
SCHOOLS." The jackets are being sold for $20.00, the shirts for $15 .00, and the
hats for $6.00. Hats and shirts are the best selling items. We are now making plans
for a vigorous campaign to distribute these items and we hope that next year we
can make a full and favorable report.

.

Masons on Campus
A pilot program has been concluded in the Los Angeles Unified School
District titled "MASONS ON CAMPUS." This program was designed to unify the
students in the classrooms and on school property by the association with adults on
campuses. This program is designed to be a year round program. Due to the
number of Masons available, the number of schools, and the diversity of the
students, people of all influences were encouraged to participate. At this time we
have a fine working relationship with the School Board of Education, the Prince
Hall Masons, the citizens in the area, and the students and staff Information
packets are available for each lodge from your Grand Lodge Public Schools
Committeeman. It is highly encouraged that each lodge adopt an annual Masons
on Campus Program.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTE E
ON TOURNAM ENT OF ROSES PARADE FLOAT

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F& A.M. ofCalifornia:

The Tournament of Roses Parade Float Committee has the responsibility of
arranging all of the details necessary to enter a Masonic Float in the Rose Parade
in Pasadena on New Year's Day.
The scope of the Committee's tasks includes the selection of the float theme,
design of the float. negotiation of a contract with the float builder, fund raising

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

from members of the Masonic fraternity on a voluntary basis, liaison with the
Tournament of Roses Committee and the float builder, selection of float riders,
publicity, float decoration, food service for the decorators, costumes,
accommodation and transportation for riders, photography and videography, design
and sales of merchandise relating to the float, and many other details.

members of Al Malaikah Shrine provided their motor homes at the start of the
Parade to keep the riders warm until it was time for them to board the float for the
5 mile journey down the Parade route. A mortuary provided limousine services for
the riders. South Pasadena Masonic Temple and Lodge made their facilities
available for the riders to change clothes and also provided lunch after the Parade.
Pasadena Temple was also made available for the youth New Year's Eve party
organized for the decorators. The committee also appreciates the devoted services
of Melissa Cronin who coordinated some of the float decorators and Saundra Coe
and Michelle Brown who manned the decorator sign-in table and merchandise sales
during the decoration period.

404

The 1994 float was titled "BUILDERS OF DEMOCRACY" in keeping with
the Parade theme "FANTASTIC ADVENTIJRES." It displayed the principal
working tools of Freemasonry and was dominated by a square and compass
reaching 17 feet above the street. The other working tools included the level,
plumb, 24-inch gauge and trowel. A scroll and quill symbolized the documents of
democracy. Books representing the knowledge required for building and the
education necessary for democracy to survive were placed at the rear of the float
beside the scroll. On the front of the float, an open book showing the DeMolay
emblem and the seven cardinal virtues of DeMolay were displayed. A single
candle towering over the book represented the seven candles used in the DeMolay
ceremonies and also sym bolized the light of Freemasonry and democracy shining
on the world, itself represented by a huge globe in the center of the float.
Four prominent riders were aboard the float. On the front, the International
Master Concilor of DeMolay, Brother David Hendricks off alls Church, Virginia
stood beside the DeMolay emblem. Behind him was Mrs. Barbara Pierce, Worthy
Grand Matron, Order of the Eastern Star, California. Seated on the right side of the
float was an 83 year old Masonic leader of one of the newest democratic societies
in Europe, Most Worshipful Nicholai Filip, Grand Master of Masons in Romania.
Occupying a standing position on the left side of the float was a George
Washington look-alike representing one of history's outstanding Masons associated
with the building of democracy. An independent committee, using only
photographs submitted by sixteen contestants without names or geographical
locations, selected Dr. Frederick T. Alexander, Past Master of Van Nuys Lodge No.
450 as the winner of this nationwide contest. As a result of his appearance on the
float, he has been invited to many organizations to speak about George Washington
and the Constitution.
Special thanks are due to a number of people or organizations for the
assistance they provided. In particular, the I 000 or so members of the Masonic
youth groups and their advisors who decorated the float did an outstanding job and
also acted as ambassadors for Freemasonry by assisting on other floats as well.
Our float was the first one completed prior to the judging on the day before the
Parade. Members of the Shrine and York Rite performed the almost impossible
task of providing hot, wholesome meals for the decorators for several days. Two

405

The 1994 float was well received by the viewing public and was financially
successful also, even though the committee was very concerned in September when
donations were far below the needs to meet expenses. Fortunately, contributions
in the last three months before the Parade enabled the committee to meet its
obligations with very little to spare. Actual net expenditures were $91 ,779,
including $75,000 for the float itself. Other expenses included the float entry fee,
publicity, correspondence, photography, video editing, accommodations, food for
decorators, costume rental and other non-recoverable miscellaneous expenses.
The television coverage on the 1994 float was significantly better than the
previous year, partly due to the commentators having generally followed a script
provided to them by the committee.
A 19 minute videotape was produced from footage provided by several
members of the committee. This tape described the relationship between
Freemasonry and democracy and the working tools of Freemasonry in addition to
showing the TV coverage provided by the CBS and NBC networks and Los
Angeles channels KTLA and KITV. Copies were sent to all Grand Lodges and
concordant bodies for future promotion of the float program and for their
educational value. An 8x I 0 color photograph of the float was also sent to
individual Lodges which contributed to the float and to every Grand Lodge and
concordant organization.
Since January 2, 1994 , our attention has been focused on the 1995 float. The
Parade theme is "SPORTS - QUEST FOR EXCELLENCE ." As our float theme,
we chose the Shrine East-West Football Game as a fund raiser for the excellent
work performed by the Shriners Hospitals and titled the float "SERVICE
THROUGH SPORTS."
As 1995 is the 75th Anniversary of the International Order of Job's Daughters,
they are being honored on the front of the float where they will form a living
triangle of three young ladies - Kay Louise Weber, Miss International Job's

406

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Daughter from Spokane, Washington; Shannon Galagan, Supreme Bethel Honored
Queen from Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada; and Karen Boerwinkle, California
Grand Bethel Honored Queen. They will be placed behind the Holy Bible
symbolically opened at the Book of Job and they will be flanked by two large
diamonds representing 75 years.
In the center of the float, the Grand Master of Masons in California (now
Deputy Grand Master William F. Stovall) will be standing between the pillars of
the Lodge and will be joined by C. Fred Kleinknecht, Sovereign Grand
Commander, Supreme Council, Scottish Rite, Southern Jurisdiction of the United
States and Blair C. Mayford, Grand Master of the Grand Encampment of Knights
Templar.
The rear portion of the float will have a replica of a football field with goal
posts spelling out SHRJNERS HOSPITALS. In front of the goal posts, the
Imperial Potentate of the Shrine of North America, Burton E. Ravellette, Jr. will
be accompanied by two football players and two children from the Shriners
Hospitals.
At the time of writing, the contributions for the 1995 float are lagging and the
Float Committee is again concerned. A special appeal for assistance has been
prepared for release after the Annual Communication.
During the year, the committee lost one of its most valuable members. Brother
Royal Dano passed away on May 15, 1994 after a long battle with emphysema. He
was a pillar of strength to the committee and worked tirelessly soliciting
contributions from Grand Lodges and other organizations. His practical and
careful approach to solving problems and his good humor endeared him to all
members of the committee. He is missed but his legacy continues.
The members of the committee have enjoyed working on one of the most
positive activities in Freemasonry and we thank the Grand Master and other
officers and Lodges for the support that they have given us during the year. We are
also grateful to the Los Angeles Scottish Rite and the Southern California DeMolay
for the use of their meeting facilities.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON TRIAL REVIEW

, To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

There have been referred to your Committee on Trial Review since the 1993
Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, seventeen trials, of which one is a carryover from the 1992 Annual Communication, and four are matters remanded for
new trial.
Your committee has reviewed each of the Trial Records numbered 2349, 2350,
2361, 2362, 2363, 2364, 2365, 2366, 2367, 2368 (formerly 2352), 2370 and 2371
and finds that in each case there was substantial compliance with procedural
requirements of our Constitution and Ordinances, and the result is supported by the
evidence in the record of each case and that there are no miscarriages of justice.
Your committee therefore moves the adoption of the following Resolution:
"RESOLVED, t~at in each of Trial Records above numbered, the judgement
and penalty imposed by and are ratified, afftrmed and approved, and that Trial
Records No. 2328, 2347, 2355 and 2359, be carried over to the next Annual
Communication.
Your committee also wants to report on two other matters. First, a Manual for
Masonic Trials has been compiled by Worshipful Thomas M. Sagar and another
by the Right Worshipful William F. Stovall. We are editing the product of these
Brothers into one manual which we believe will be of great help to Lodges and
Trial Masters. The Grand Secretary will mail our draft of the Manual when a copy
of the charges has been forwarded to his office.
Second, last year the Annual Communication adopted modifications of
Masonic Trial Procedure. One of them charged this committee with the duty of
obtaining able Trial Masters. We solicited the help of Inspectors and others in

PROCEEDTNGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Grand Lodge so that we could have a list of capable people. That effort has not
been successful. We need your help in that we need the nomination by you of Past
Masters in your area believed by you to be capable of conducting a trial. Do not
be put off by this. We will screen such people. We will also train them, as needed.
So, please, help us have a list from which the Grand Master can appoint a Trial
Master in any area of this jurisdiction.

level of conduct and contact involving the daughters, sisters, mothers and widows
of our brother Masons than the criminal laws demand. Your committee finds that
the Trial Commissioners committed a gross violation of Masonic law in accordance
with California Masonic Code Section 33030. Our Code authorizes the Grand
Lodge to reverse not guilty verdicts when it finds that a gross violation of law
occurs. The Code also authorizes the Grand Lodge to take any action it deems
appropriate in accordance with California Masonic Code Section 330 I 0.

408

Trial Record No. 2369
In Trial Record No. 2369, a member of Kaweah Lodge No. 665 was charged
with six specifications of unmasonic conduct.
In the Tulare County Municipal Court, the accused was charged with sexual
battery. As a result of a plea bargain the accused pied nolo contendere and was
found guilty of one count of243 .4 P.C. (Sexual Battery), on January 24, 1994. The
accused was found guilty of rubbing his erect genitals, while fully clothed, against
the body of the victim. The accused was placed on probation, ordered to pay a
fine, incarcerated for three days, perfonn public service (200 hours) and to stay
away from the victims, including meetings involving the victims at the Masonic
Temple.
Subsequent to the criminal trial, the accused pied not guilty to the unrnasonic
A Masonic Trial was held that resulted in the Trial
conduct charges.
Commissioners finding the accused not guilty.
In reviewing the case your committee noted the following facts. The accused
was acting as a DeMolay chaperone at a joint DeMolay/Job's Daughter trip to a
lake. During the course of that outing the accused's behavior towards the Job's
Daughters on his house boat raised some concern among the chaperones. The
chaperones talked to several Job's Daughters at which time six of them made the
allegations that resulted in both criminal and unmasonic charges being filed.
Your committee noted that our Code very clearly states that a conviction in a
criminal court is prima facia e vidence in a Masonic Trial that the criminal act did
occur. Your committee also received infonnation that Trial Commissioners were
contacted by supporters of the accused and other Trial Commissioners and asked
to go easy on him because of his work with the Eastern Star.
Your committee after careful review of this case believes that a gross
miscarriage of justice has taken place. The facts are clear, the accused has been
found guilty in a criminal court of unlawful sexual contact with a female . The
victim is a Job's Daughter who was on a trip at which the accused was one of the
adult chaperones. Clearly, our Code of conduct and obligations demand a higher

409

Your committee therefore submits the following Resolution:
RESOLVED, that in Trial Record No. 2369 the finding of not guilty be
reversed, that a finding of guilty be entered, and the penalty be set at
Expulsion.
Respectfully submitted,
Donald R. Fretz, Chairman

'REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON WARDENS' MANAGEMENT RETREATS

To rhe Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The Wardens Weekend Management Retreat Program continues to be one of
the most successful programs in our Grand Lodge. This year we trained a total
of235 Senior Wardens and 163 of their ladies, and 211 Junior Wardens and
139 of their ladies. These numbers equate to a twelve percent (12%) increase
in the number of Wardens attending, and for the first time in the history of the
Retreats we are reaching over fifty percent (50%) of the Lodges in our Grand
Jurisdiction . The following is a breakdown of the Retreats:

410

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Senior Wardens Retreat - North - 115 Wardens and 85 Ladies March 4-7, 1994
- San Ramon Marriott Hotel
Senior Wardens Retreat - South - 120 Wardens and 78 Ladies March 11-13
1994 - Holiday Inn Crown Plaza, LAX Airport
'
Junior Wardens Retreat - South - I 04 Wardens and 69 Ladies April 29-May
1, 1994 - Holiday Inn Crown Plaza, LAX Airport
Junior Wardens Retreat - North - 107 Wardens and 70 Ladies May 13-15,
1994 - San Ramon Marriott Hotel
The Senior Wardens' Retreats were under the direction of our Deputy Grand
Master, William F. Stovall, and his Lady Beverly, and were extremely successful.
These Retreats were built around Brother Bill's theme, "Freemasonry - For God,
For Country, For Family." Leadership training was provided in the areas of
Financial Planning, New Member Orientation, Youth Activities, Communications,
Getting People to Volunteer, Freemasonry and Religion. These subjects were
reinforced with the Wardens by the use of Team Building Exercises and Group
Reports. The ladies participated in many of the above subjects with their husbands
and in addition covered subjects on Planning an Installation and the Role of the
Master's Wife.
The Junior Wardens' Retreats were under the direction of our Senior Grand
Warden, Charles H. Alexander, and his Lady Greta. Subjects covered in these
Retreats included Leadership and Change, In Search of Excellence, Planning Your
Year as Master, Interesting More People in Masonry, Masonic Protocol, How to
Get Things Done, Planning a Good Event and many more. Jn addition the ladies
received training in the History of Freemasonry and the Role of the Master's Wife.
This training was reinforced with Team Building Exercises and Group Reports.
The Junior Wardens and their ladies left these Retreats with a better understanding
of freemasonry, their leadership role in the Lodge and how to make their Lodges
successful.
Speakers used in these sessions included William Stovall, Charles Alexander,
Allen Gresham, Victor Howard, Stanley Cazneaux, Larry Coyle, Loyal Stark and
Robert Winterton, Sr. Each did an outstanding job and were well received by those
in attendance. The ladies speakers included Beverly Stovall, Greta Alexander,
Gloria Cazneaux and Shirley Coyle. I want to thank each of these ladies for their

41 I

participation and an excellent job.
A special thank you must go the Brother and Doctor Victor Howard, our Staff
Clinical Psychologist, for his outstanding contributions to the success of these
Retreats. His excellent presentations are well accepted by those in attendance. He
is responsible for the development of the Work Exercises used in the Breakaway
Sessions. His knowledge in Management Organization and Leadership Skills have
been a major reason for the success of the Retreats.
Once again this year I want to thank Robert Winterton, Sr., Inspector of the
497th Masonic District, for his significant contribution to the Wardens' Retreat
Program. Brother Bob has been involved in these Retreats since their inception and
has spoken at every session over the past six years. He is an exceptional speaker
with the ability to mix good humor with a hard-hitting message. His contribution
to the success of these Retreats is immeasurable.
I extend my deep appreciation to Richard "Hap" Arnold who handles the
logistics at the Southern California Retreats, and to Michael Gonsolin, Inspector of
the 153rd Masonic District, who performs the same function in the North. They
both provide great support to the Retreats. A very special thank you is extended
to Kimberly Weisser of the Grand Lodge Office Staff, for the outstanding clerical
support she has provided the Retreats. She always provides quality materials in a
very professional manner.
For myself, I want to once again express my deep appreciation to the members
of the committee for their dedication to this important program. One important
member of the committee whose name does not appear in the Grand Lodge Roster
is that of Gloria Cazneaux. Without her assistance and long hours of work, I would
never to able to ac·complish all the tasks necessary to make these Retreats
successful. I deeply appreciate her assistance and continued support of
Freemasonry.
Respectfully submitted,
Stanley M. Cazneaux, PGM, Chairman
